title: Book 12 opens: why Levi’s chosen priests were still examined
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK TWELVE. On the priesthood.

Cyril: We have now spoken plainly about the sacred vestment, and also about the sacrifices which God ordained must be carried out at the consecration of the priests. But since countless things were declared in the oracles concerning them, about their ministry and purifications, and about the exact propriety they need if they are to live in strictest keeping with the law, polished to a spiritual refinement, I think I must say one thing before all the rest.
Palladius: What is that?

Cyril: The tribe sprung from the blood of Levi was an offering dedicated to God and chosen out of all the tribes, and the law gave this family the duty of serving as priests, God granting it this honor as its special portion. Yet he did not leave the priestly company altogether unexamined, nor did he simply open the office to anyone at all on the ground that he was of Levi’s blood. He ordered that they be inquired into, and very minutely, so that no one who happened to suffer one of the censured defects should be unacceptable to God and make his approach blemished, and, all but rushing into the tent of witness with unwashed feet (Exodus 30:19–21), give offence, even without meaning to. And again it is written thus in Leviticus (Leviticus 21:16–19): ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Say to Aaron: A man of your family throughout your generations who has a blemish in him shall not come near to offer the gifts of his God. No man who has a blemish in him shall come near: a man who is blind, or lame, or has a stunted nose, or a clipped ear, or a man who has
translator_notes: PG 68.781. Opening speech is Cyril’s; the Greek has no speaker marker, but Palladius answers it, so it carries the ‘Cyril:’ label, as in Books 8 and 11. κεχρησμῳδημένων rendered ‘declared in the oracles’ (God’s legal pronouncements). Unwashed feet in the tent of witness: clear allusion to the laver rule (Exodus 30:19–21; the LXX also uses σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου), cited. The Leviticus quotation is LXX 21:16–19 and runs on into §2; its citation is placed beside the introducing clause because the section breaks mid-verse (PG column cut kept). κολοβόρινος rendered ‘stunted nose’ (Cyril later explains it as σιμότης, a flattened nose); ὠτότμητος ‘clipped ear’ (LXX plus; not in the Hebrew of Leviticus 21:18).

title: Bodily defects are not sin but figures of the soul’s faults
english: Cyril: …a broken hand or a broken foot, or is hunchbacked, or has a white spot on his eye, or has lost his eyelashes, or a man who has a malignant scab, or a scaly rash, or has only one testicle. No one of the seed of Aaron the priest who has a blemish in him shall draw near to offer the sacrifices to the Lord, because there is a blemish in him. He shall not come near to offer the gifts of his God. He shall eat the gifts of his God, the most holy things, and of the holy things; but he shall not come near to the veil, and he shall not draw near to the altar, because he has a blemish; and he shall not profane the sanctuary of his God, for I am the Lord who sanctifies them.’ (Leviticus 21:19–23)
Palladius: Tell me, then: is bodily infirmity held as a charge against anyone? Does the Creator indict nature even when it has been impaired against its will?

Cyril: Well said, Palladius; you think rightly. Blame and indictment may sometimes fall on those whose minds turn aside to evil of their own free choice, and who have come to prize a leaning toward outrage of any kind. But to censure infirmities of the flesh, which come about by nature and against the will, is, I think, harsh and unfeeling, and not free from the charge of crassness. From this, then, we can understand that the Creator of all would not have indicted human nature for causes beyond the will, nor would he have sent away from the ministry appointed to him, as unholy, a man who is sick in body. Rather, once more, by a type drawn from bodily things he refines our minds toward his subtler purposes: he hints at the many forms of the passions in the soul and gives us to understand that such a thing is hateful to God. Did not the inspired Paul also say that those chosen for the priesthood must be attended by an honorable verdict on every quality that wins admiration? ‘So that the man of God may be complete,’ he says, ‘fully equipped for every good work’ (2 Timothy 3:17). He insisted, too, and very clearly, that the bishop must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2), and he was very exacting in these matters.
Palladius: I agree. Next, believe me, I would very much like to learn the meaning of each of the infirmities we have just listed.

Cyril: Come, then, let us take them one at a time, each in its kind, and say what comes to mind. ‘A man,’ it says, ‘throughout your generations, of your family, who has a blemish in him, shall not come near to offer the gifts of his God’ (Leviticus 21:17). The word is firm, the decree severe. For the law was laid down not only for those born of Aaron at that time; it reaches to the whole family and to every priestly line, and it extends through all time. That, I think, is what ‘of your family throughout your generations’ makes clear. For what is not blameless is always unacceptable to God. And no one could name a time when what has been condemned would become dear to him, above all in the case of spiritual infirmities;
translator_notes: PG 68.784. Section opens mid-quotation (Leviticus 21:19), continuing Cyril’s speech from §1. LXX blemish terms: ἔφηλος ‘white spot on the eye’ (LSJ leucoma), πτιλὸς τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς ‘has lost his eyelashes’, ψώρα ἀγρία ‘malignant scab’, λιχήν ‘scaly rash’, μονόρχης ‘only one testicle’ (Hebrew differs at several points; English follows Cyril’s LXX). Γράφεται / γραφή taken in the legal sense ‘indict / indictment’. σκαιότης rendered ‘perversity’ (boorish wrongheadedness). ‘Honorable verdict … on every quality that is admired’ (εὐκλεᾶ ψῆφον) may echo 1 Timothy 3:7 (‘a good testimony from outsiders’), but the wording is not close: left uncited. ‘Above reproach’ = ἀνεπίληπτον, the word of 1 Timothy 3:2 (Titus 1:7 has ἀνέγκλητον), cited 1 Timothy 3:2. The final clause (ὡς ἐπ’ ἀρρωστίαις … πνευματικαῖς) runs on into §3.

title: The blameless priesthood in Christ; what the blind and the lame signify
english: Cyril: …rather, what he holds in honor is the blameless: what suffers no corruption from any quarter, what is sound, so to speak, in virtue and strong in sanctification, what has trained itself thoroughly to win approval through patient endurance, and is always quick to understand. That is why he makes his law on this point extend to the whole family, showing the sacred and chosen race to be his own and free of all alloy: then, in the tribe of Levi and the blood of Aaron; but now in those who have been sanctified in Christ, the great and true High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), to whom we have been joined through the Spirit, and so have been shown to be sharers and partakers of his own nature (2 Peter 1:4). So too, having called into brotherhood those who have been justified by faith (Hebrews 2:11), he rejoices over them as sharers with him, saying: ‘Here am I, and the children whom God has given me’ (Hebrews 2:13; Isaiah 8:18). Or did not the inspired Paul see fit to attach this saying, too, to the person of Christ?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: He bars from serving as priest, then, anyone with any of the defects named, as infirm and open to ridicule. For it says, ‘A man who is blind or lame shall not come near to offer the gifts of God’ (Leviticus 21:17–18). Now even taken in a bodily sense, the matter plainly has much that is unseemly. For when the eyes have wasted away, and the foot is not firm and cannot walk straight, is it not better for the priest to keep still, since he cannot even tell where he ought to go, rather than to go about amid laughter, using another’s foot and another’s eyes? But we need not say much about that. Let us rather speak of what we need for knowledge and spiritual contemplation, getting beneath the coarse surface of the history. By ‘blind,’ then, he seems to mean the man who is very foolish and utterly senseless. For what the eye is to the earthly body, the mind may be called in the soul. It is lit up by the divine light, it opens its eyes to that pure beauty itself, and with the fine and nimble movements, as it were, of its thoughts it springs up readily toward exact belief, and knows how to keep from missing right doctrine. This, I think, is what is said in the Proverbs: ‘Let your eyes look straight, and let your eyelids nod toward what is just’ (Proverbs 4:25). And somewhere it is also said to the mother of the Jews, who did not see rightly: ‘See, your eyes are not good, nor is your heart; they are set on nothing but your greed, on innocent blood, to shed it, on your wrongdoings, and on murder, to commit them’ (Jeremiah 22:17). So the one who is blind in the spiritual sense is unfit for sacred service, that is, the man wholly without understanding, maimed in mind and judgment. Unfit as well is the lame man, that is, one who does not know how to walk uprightly and has no strength to walk soundly. For blindness, as I said just now, is a sign of utter lack of understanding; lameness, in turn, is a sign of a movement and eagerness that is, as it were, broken and feeble, such as a man may show toward each of the things he has to do. Unless it is right to call out to those so maimed:
translator_notes: PG 68.785. ‘Great … High Priest’ echoes Hebrews 4:14 (ἀρχιερέα μέγαν); ‘sharers … of his own nature’ echoes 2 Peter 1:4 (κοινωνοὶ φύσεως); ‘called into brotherhood’ echoes Hebrews 2:11 just before the quoted Hebrews 2:13 (itself from Isaiah 8:18): all cited. ‘Chosen race’ (ἀπόλεκτον γένος) may echo 1 Peter 2:9, but Cyril’s word differs (ἐκλεκτόν there): left uncited. ‘Spirit’ (διὰ πνεύματος) read as the Holy Spirit, by Cyril’s usual teaching on union with Christ. Cyril takes Hebrews as Paul’s. Proverbs 4:25 has the same number in LXX and English. Jeremiah 22:17 in context is addressed to the king (Jehoiakim/Shallum); Cyril reads it as said to ‘the mother of the Jews’ (Jerusalem): kept as he has it. ὀρθοποδεῖν (‘walk uprightly’) may echo Galatians 2:14, but the passage is about the lameness type, so left uncited. ἤγουν in the laughter sentence read as comparative (‘rather than’). The sentence ending ‘call out to those so maimed:’ leads into the Isaiah quotation that opens §4.

title: Weak hands, the flattened nose and the clipped ear
english: Cyril: ‘Be strong, you slack hands and paralysed knees’ (Isaiah 35:3). And Christ himself accused the Jewish people of refusing to make their paths toward him straight, letting them turn aside instead into lameness (Hebrews 12:13), and of slipping away from right reasoning. ‘For foreign sons,’ he says, ‘lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped away from their paths’ (Psalm 18:44–45). So lameness of mind and blindness are on a par and very close to each other, being afflictions alike in kind: blindness reduces to uselessness what is precious in understanding, and lameness what is strong in good works. Besides these, the law said that the man with a stunted nose must be rejected, and with him the man with a clipped ear. One might apply to them an explanation like this. By the sense of smell we test what smells foul and what is most fragrant, among things, I mean, whose nature has received the power to give off a smell; and that sense is very discerning, both of what can give delight and of what perhaps is not of that sort but otherwise, ranking, as it were, among the worse. The human mind, I would say, if it is sound in what belongs to it, sets out vigorously to discern the quality of things and will make an exact test of each; and like an excellent money-changer, testing everything, holding fast to what is good and keeping away from every form of evil, as it is written (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22), it will win high approval. For it rejects as counterfeit whatever among our deeds is in any way shameful and falsely stamped, and it would readily accept what is profitable and better. The flattened nose, then, signifies what is not altogether healthy and sound in perception, the faculty by which we discern each thing excellently, give the better verdict to the best and the worse to the more shameful, and are, and are called, wise and quick-witted and everything else of that kind. For the smell, rising as it were to the mind, is the real quality, so to speak, of the things the mind perceives. And to have the ear clipped would suggest, as it seems to me, being hard of hearing. For when the hearing is clipped, I would grant that the affliction is an obedience given only in part, not wholly answering to the rein, or else the inability to listen blamelessly to sacred things, and above all to the sacred writings. Some indeed do just that, most thoughtlessly turning the soul’s readiness to hear toward things it should not. These would be, in the words of the most wise Paul, those who have itching ears and turn their hearing away from the truth (2 Timothy 4:3–4), who devote themselves to spirits of error (1 Timothy 4:1), and who have turned aside to profane, empty talk (1 Timothy 6:20). So the man with a clipped ear would suggest the maiming of the inward and spiritual hearing, and its corruption from rightness into something worse. And if anyone is seen to have a broken foot or a broken hand (Leviticus 21:19), let him withdraw, it says, and be ranked with the others; and here the law leads us to understand, by the man whose foot or hand may have been broken but who is not wholly disabled,
translator_notes: PG 68.788. Isaiah 35:3 is quoted in LXX form (also behind Hebrews 12:12). ‘Make straight paths … lameness … turned aside’ is Hebrews 12:13 (τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιεῖτε … τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ), cited as an allusion in Cyril’s wording, not as Christ’s words; the words Cyril assigns to Christ are the Psalm quotation that follows. Psalm: LXX Psalm 17:45b–46 = English Psalm 18:44b–45. ἡ μὲν … ἡ δὲ resolved by sense (blindness → understanding, lameness → works, as in §3), not by word order. The money-changer image echoes the well-known saying ‘be approved money-changers’ (an unwritten saying, not in the canon), joined here to 1 Thessalonians 5:21–22, which Cyril marks with ‘as it is written’; only 1 Thessalonians is cited. νοῦς γε μὴν ἔφη: ἔφη is odd (perhaps for ἔφην or φημί); rendered ‘I would say’, doubtful reading. κατακιβδηλεύει normally ‘adulterates’; here by context ‘rejects as counterfeit’ (assaying image). ἱερῶν … γραμμάτων ‘sacred writings’ may echo 2 Timothy 3:15 (ἱερὰ γράμματα), a stock phrase: uncited. ‘Spirits of error’: 1 Timothy 4:1 (πνεύμασιν πλάνοις; compare 1 John 4:6), cited 1 Timothy 4:1 since Cyril names Paul; ‘profane empty talk’ also in 2 Timothy 2:16, cited 1 Timothy 6:20 (ἐκτρεπόμενος matches ‘turned aside’). ‘Let him withdraw … same footing as the others’ is Cyril’s paraphrase (φησίν) of the law, not LXX wording; the broken hand/foot is Leviticus 21:19. Ends mid-sentence before §5 τὸν οὐχ ὁλοκλήρως; PG column cut kept.

title: Halting deeds, the bent back, and sin done openly
english: Cyril: …the one who cannot carry his deeds through to the full, and whose walk, that is, his activity, is not entirely beyond reproach: I mean in conduct and in a life lived fully by the law. These again would be those who do the work of the Lord carelessly, against whom the voice of the prophet has pronounced woe (Jeremiah 48:10), or those who pursue what is just, but not justly, as it is written (Deuteronomy 16:20). Notice that even a moderate injury to the leg is put on the same level as spiritual and complete lameness, and is counted as the same thing. For not doing good rightly will be placed on the same footing as being unable to do any good at all. One may fairly see in lameness the ‘not at all,’ and in the crushed limb the ‘not soundly.’
Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: Again, he lists the hunchback, the man with blotches, and the man with bleary eyes among the most unfit (Leviticus 21:20). We say the hunchback is the one who is, as it were, bent over: he looks downward in mind, leans toward the passions of the flesh, and fixes his eye on earthly things (clearly, the eye of the mind), and has at last come to such a frame of mind that he hates to be set upright, I mean, for the duty of setting the mind on things above (Colossians 3:2). Under this would fall the charges against the Jews, of whom it is written: ‘Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back for ever’ (Psalm 69:23; Romans 11:10). The man with blotches is one who has what is called a blotch on his very forehead. This is a kind of sickness that darkens the surface of the skin. It takes from those who suffer it even the chance of staying hidden, since it breaks out on the very brows and spreads over the whole face. Such a man, then, is blotched in body; but in a spiritual sense he points to the man who is unseemly openly and without concealment, who has, as it were, no clean face, but whose ugliness of life is plain to all, so that perhaps he does not even know what one of the wise rightly said: ‘The wise will hide their own shames.’
Palladius: What do you mean?
Cyril: Are there not, Palladius, countless passions in us?
Palladius: Yes. What of it?

Cyril: This, my good friend: each of us is sick with his own sickness, but often, overcome by shame before his brothers, he takes great pains and care both to seem healthy and to keep his faults out of sight.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: But suppose someone has come to such shamelessness that he thinks nothing of choosing to sin openly and of throwing away entirely the honors that belong to a decent life. Would not anyone think that such a man has gone far from the sacred and holy race?
Palladius: Very much so.
Cyril: The law, then, calls such a man blotched, since he neither knows how to hide nor will bear to hide the sickness and passion that has come upon him. And the man with bleary
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, continuing Leviticus 21:19 (crushed foot or hand) from section 4. Jeremiah 48:10 = LXX Jeremiah 31:10, which reads 'cursed (ἐπικατάρατος) is he who does the works of the Lord carelessly'; Cyril calls it 'the woe' (τὸ οὐαί), so 'woe' is kept as his word. 'Pursue what is just, but not justly' inverts LXX Deuteronomy 16:20 'δικαίως τὸ δίκαιον διώξῃ' (justly pursue what is just). Psalm 69:23 = LXX Psalm 68:24; the same wording is quoted at Romans 11:10, and Cyril's framing (charges against the Jews) echoes Paul. 'Setting the mind on things above' (τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖν) is Colossians 3:2. 'The wise will hide their own shames' is introduced as 'one of the wise' and has no exact LXX match (Proverbs 10:14 LXX begins 'σοφοὶ κρύψουσιν αἴσθησιν', 'the wise will hide discernment'); left uncited. Lev 21:20 terms: κυρτός hunchback; ἔφηλος, which Cyril explains as a dark blotch (ἐφηλίς) on the forehead and face (LXX sense is probably a white speck in the eye, but his reading governs), rendered 'with blotches'; πτίλος τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, eyes that have lost their lashes, rendered 'bleary eyes' to fit his reading in section 6 (sees, but not soundly). The paragraph ends mid-phrase ('Πτιλὸν δὲ τοὺς | ὀφθαλμούς'); section 6 opens '…eyes'.

title: Bleary eyes, the raging itch, and the spreading rash
english: Cyril: …eyes is the one who is by no means deprived of sight, yet cannot see soundly. Such would be those who have understanding, but in whom no choice to think rightly is seen. For some, he means, see what is good, yet turn the bent of their own wills aside toward what they ought not; others, though they could have a share in right doctrine, all but ruin their own minds themselves: they throw themselves into a most unlovely hunt after notions and accept nothing sound in their belief about God. Such above all are the children of the heretics, and the Jews besides, who believe that the Father is God, yet most foolishly thrust away the One who has come forth from him, the Son by nature. So the word proclaimed by the voice of the prophet is true of them: ‘They have eyes, and they do not see’ (Jeremiah 5:21). For seeing is of no use unless care is taken that one sees soundly, just as we rightly said that lameness and the crushed foot are placed on the same footing. For it will make no difference at all whether one cannot walk at all or perhaps does not walk soundly, meaning, of course, the path of conduct and the road of deeds.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: ‘No man shall come near to serve as priest who has a raging itch or a spreading rash on him, or who has only one testicle, or anyone who has any blemish in him’ (Leviticus 21:20–21). We should liken the raging itch to the most monstrous of the passions, which pour down on the mind in sharper, more acrid streams and pass all measure, and which begin in pleasure but end in bitterness. Or would you not say that in each kind of sin the evil is seen in a measured form and also beyond measure?
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: The man overcome by bodily pleasure: could he not suffer this both moderately and beyond measure? Some are only overcome, and are sick in a restrained way; others reach the height of the evil and are sick with a pleasure that rages out of control, so that they slip even beyond the passions that belong to nature.
Palladius: I understand what you mean.

Cyril: So in each of the evils, whatever has strayed monstrously beyond reason, and beyond the measures that are usual and common among most people, may be called the raging itch. The spreading rash, besides, is any passion at all that keeps creeping outward over a wider area and never stops growing worse. But the divine law wants us to check the passions that befall us and to reduce them. You will understand something of this kind when you hear: ‘If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for healing will put an end to great sins’ (Ecclesiastes 10:4). For passions left unrebuked always creep toward a more shameful state; they seize heart and mind and lead to utter ruin. So we must rebuke what is base, while the sobriety within us, by turning back again toward what is better, keeps it
translator_notes: 'They have eyes, and they do not see' matches LXX Jeremiah 5:21 word for word (ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῖς καὶ οὐ βλέπουσιν), and 'through the voice of the prophet' fits Jeremiah; the verb ὑμνούμενον ('sung') could suggest the Psalms (Psalm 115:5 = LXX 113:13, 'ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχουσιν καὶ οὐκ ὄψονται'), but the wording points to Jeremiah. 'He means' renders an unclear φησί in 'Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ὁρῶντες, φησὶ'. 'Son by nature' keeps κατὰ φύσιν Υἱόν (Cyril's anti-Arian term). Leviticus 21:20–21: ψώρα ἀγρία rendered 'raging itch' to keep Cyril's play with ἀγριαίνουσαν ('rages'); λειχήν rendered 'spreading rash' to match his gloss (διέρπον εἰς τὸ εὐρύ); μόνορχις 'only one testicle'. 'The passions that belong to nature' (τῶν κατὰ φύσιν παθῶν) may hint at unnatural vice (cf. Romans 1:26–27) but no citation is given. Ecclesiastes 10:4 is cited verbatim from the LXX; 'the spirit of the ruler' is the ruler's anger, which Cyril applies to an assault of passion. The section ends inside a genitive absolute (περιστελ|λούσης); section 7 opens '…in check'.

title: The half-man and the holy food: what the blemished may receive
english: Cyril: …in check and destroys it little by little. Next, as I at least think, he means by the man with only one testicle the half-man, the one who has, as it were, been cut off from full manliness. ‘For neither the sexually immoral,’ he says, ‘nor the soft will inherit the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 6:9–10). By this he names the effeminate, because, though they were given the nature of a man, they belie their manhood: they grow soft in mind and body and willingly break themselves down into feebleness and womanish ways. It is likely, again, that the man with one testicle points to something else as well. For it is usual to call a ‘man’ one who is strong and well knit, and fully able to accomplish whatever he may choose. So a half-man may fittingly be understood as one who is not wholly strong, nor fully vigorous for what befits him. For it is not fitting that one devoted to God should bring him a courage cut short and a strength maimed, so as to be weak in part; rather he should ‘act like a man and be strong,’ as it is written (1 Corinthians 16:13), with an eagerness that no one can fault or mock. So the man listed under ‘blemish’ is admittedly unfit for sacred service. Yet he is not barred from sharing in the holy food. ‘For he shall eat of the holy things,’ he says, ‘but he shall not go in to the veil, and he shall not come near the altar’ (Leviticus 21:22–23). For those who are still subject to weaknesses hidden within the mind may share in the blessing of Christ, not as ranked among the saints, for growth in holiness, for steadiness of mind, and for a steadfastness firmly grounded in all that is best, but in the way that suits the sick: for the putting away of evil, the ending of sin, the putting to death of pleasures, and the recovery of spiritual health. For since Christ is a new creation, according to the Scriptures (2 Corinthians 5:17), we too therefore receive him into ourselves through his holy flesh and blood, so that, refashioned through him and in him for newness of life (Romans 6:4), we may put off the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit, as it is written (Ephesians 4:22).
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: So he forbids the practice of sacred duties to those who are sick with a spiritual affliction that is, as it were, ingrained and cannot be thrown off; for what is always sick with passions grown into it is not holy at all. But if one of those who are blameless in themselves and beyond reproach in their ministry happens to suffer these common passions, which do not fade away, he commands that he must not be left unrebuked, saying (Leviticus 22:2–3): ‘Speak to Aaron and to his sons, and let them keep away from the holy things of the sons of Israel, and they shall not profane my holy name in what they themselves consecrate to me: I am the Lord. Say to them: Throughout your generations, any man from all your offspring who comes near
translator_notes: 1 Corinthians 6:9–10: μαλακοί rendered 'the soft' so that Cyril's next word, θηλυδρίας ('womanish'), reads as his own gloss on it. 'Act like a man and be strong' (ἀνδρίζεσθαι καὶ κραταιοῦσθαι) is cited as 1 Corinthians 16:13 (ἀνδρίζεσθε, κραταιοῦσθε); close parallels are Psalm 31:24 (LXX 30:25) and Deuteronomy 31:6. 'Christ is a new creation, according to the Scriptures' alludes to 2 Corinthians 5:17 (cf. Galatians 6:15), though Paul's text says that whoever is in Christ is a new creation. 'Newness of life' is Romans 6:4; 'the old man … corrupted according to the desires of deceit' is Ephesians 4:22 nearly verbatim. 'The blessing of Christ' (εὐλογία Χριστοῦ) is Cyril's usual term for the Eucharist, as the next sentence (his holy flesh and blood) shows; kept literal. 'Which do not fade away of themselves' renders οὐκ ἐξίτηλα (not fading, lasting); the sense seems to be passions that need cleansing rather than wearing off, but the phrase is doubtful against the contrast with 'ingrained' passions. 'Keep away from' renders προσεχέτωσαν ἀπό (LXX for Hebrew 'separate themselves from'). The quotation of Leviticus 22:2–9 runs on into section 8; the citation for its first part is placed at 'saying' because the quote stays open at the section break.

title: Uncleanness that keeps a priest from the holy things
english: Cyril: …to the holy things that the sons of Israel consecrate to the Lord while his uncleanness is on him, that soul shall be cut off from me: I am the Lord your God. And any man of the offspring of Aaron the priest who is a leper or has a discharge shall not eat of the holy things until he is cleansed; and whoever touches any uncleanness of a person, or a man from whom an emission of seed goes out, or whoever touches any unclean creeping thing that defiles him, or a human being by whom he is defiled through any uncleanness of his: the soul that touches them shall be unclean until evening. He shall not eat of the holy things unless he bathes his body in water; and when the sun sets he shall be clean, and then he shall eat of the holy things, for it is his bread. He shall not eat what has died of itself or been torn by beasts, so that he is not defiled by them: I am the Lord. And they shall keep my charges, so that they do not incur sin because of them and die because of them, if they profane them. I am the Lord who sanctifies them’ (Leviticus 22:3–9). For those who bring the sacred offerings, he says, that is, the things consecrated by the sons of Israel, whatever they dedicate to God as sacrifice, must not profane his name by bringing them without first being purified, while the uncleanness they may have contracted is still unwashed; otherwise, he says, let them know that they will at once pay the utmost penalty. For ‘I am the Lord’: that is, not a falsely named god, against whom, even if someone happened to sin, there would be no offence. For what wrong could we do to wood or stone that would make us answerable? So, adding correction to these severe threats as a safeguard against uncleanness, he usefully lists the ways in which we might incur it, so that the ministers might know the way of the uprightness that best befits them, and how they may be acceptable and clean as they walk through the life most pleasing to the Lawgiver.
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: So he removes the leper and the man with a discharge from the sacred ministry, and says that he must have no share in the holy things until he has thrown off what befell him and is wholly free of the sickness. To these he adds, as sick with an uncleanness of the same kind, the man who touches any uncleanness of a person, or from whom an emission of seed goes out, and also the one who touches a creeping thing, or touches a man who has any discharge that defiles. The law does not, I think, rebuke bodily conditions, in its true and faultless aim; rather, still in types that belong to the senses and the body, it shows what happens in souls. Leprosy, then, is a symbol of deadness; for it eats away and devours the flesh, changes it into what is against nature, and alters the appearance of the body. A discharge of seed is a casting away of the power to bear fruit, as nature flows away into nothing. Such, one might see, is a man’s mind too, when it has been led astray into corruption and is all but wasted away into barrenness, through being unable to understand any of the things
translator_notes: The quotation is LXX Leviticus 22:3–9, checked clause by clause; it opened in section 7 (Leviticus 22:2–3). 'Any uncleanness of a person' renders πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας ψυχῆς: in the Hebrew and LXX ψυχή here means a dead person (a corpse), but Cyril in section 9 reads the clause as touching those who are sick (the leper and the man with a discharge), so the neutral 'person' is kept rather than 'corpse'. 'For I am the Lord' repeats the refrain of the quoted verses and gets no separate citation. 'Lawgiver' (νομοθέτης) here means God. The section ends inside the word ἀναγ|καίων; section 9 opens '…necessary for salvation'.

title: Touching the unclean: sharing in another’s sin
english: Cyril: …necessary for salvation. Such were Hymenaeus and Alexander (1 Timothy 1:20), who both thought and said that the resurrection had already taken place (2 Timothy 2:17–18). To these may be added those who turn without restraint toward every kind of outrage, and simply throw away the fruit of their own minds on stale and wanton pleasures. So the leper and the man with a discharge, that is, the one held fast by the works of deadness (and the works of deadness would be the passions of the flesh), and the one who does not keep his inner fruitfulness uncorrupted, the hidden fruitfulness of the mind, must withdraw, he says, from the holy things until he is cleansed (Leviticus 22:4). For as the inspired Paul said, ‘Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning his body’ (1 Corinthians 11:27, 29). ‘But let a man,’ he says, ‘examine himself, and then let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup’ (1 Corinthians 11:28).
Palladius: Excellently said.

Cyril: Notice, then, Palladius, how precise the law is. It does not stop at the leper and the man with a discharge alone, but condemns along with them, as it were, anyone who happens to touch those who are sick, I mean the leper and the man with a discharge. ‘And whoever touches,’ he says, ‘anything unclean from a person, or one from whom an emission of semen goes out, shall be unclean’ (Leviticus 22:4).
Palladius: And what harm could come from this to those who touch them?

Cyril: None at all, if we take the words at face value, for a touch of the body will not defile a person’s soul. But the law is spiritual (Romans 7:14), and once again it teaches us in figures that those who are guilty of the passions of the soul are unclean, charged with defilement; and those who touch them, or cling to them, are defiled together with them, clearly by the bond of a shared will or shared deeds. For ‘bad company ruins good character’ (1 Corinthians 15:33), and ‘a believer has no share with an unbeliever’ (2 Corinthians 6:15), and light is hostile to darkness and can make no terms with it (2 Corinthians 6:14). It is true, too, that ‘with the holy you will be made holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the crooked you will turn crooked’ (Psalm 18:25–26). He showed at once that to be sick with the most outrageous of the passions will be grievous not for the sick alone, but that those who come to share their mind and judgment will be defiled with stains no less than theirs, for he added: ‘Whoever touches any unclean creeping thing, it will defile him, or a man through whom he will be defiled by any of his uncleanness; the soul that touches them shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 22:5–6). We say that the bitter and venomous creeping things, in name and in fact, are those whom this saying would fit: ‘The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness’ (Romans 3:13–14). And these would be, before all others, those who twist what is right and drum into simpler people a teaching that leads to ruin, carrying them off to thoughts that are not good and to a twisted opinion about God…
translator_notes: Opens mid-word: §8 ends ἀναγ-, §9 begins -καίων εἰς σωτηρίαν, so the first turn starts '…necessary for salvation'. Hymenaeus and Alexander are paired in 1 Timothy 1:20, but the saying that the resurrection has already happened belongs to Hymenaeus and Philetus in 2 Timothy 2:17–18; Cyril merges the two, and both are cited. 'Until he is cleansed' is Leviticus 22:4 (ἕως ἂν καθαρισθῇ). The Pauline quotation is a free blend: 'the body of the Lord' and 'his cup' are Cyril's wording, the clause 'eats and drinks judgment… not discerning the body' is 11:29, the 'unworthily' frame is 11:27; 11:28 follows. Leviticus 22:4 πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας ψυχῆς: in the Hebrew this is corpse-uncleanness; Cyril reads ψυχή as 'a person' and applies it to touching the leper and the man with a discharge, so the English keeps 'anything unclean from a person'. Psalm 17:26–27 LXX = Psalm 18:25–26 English (also 2 Samuel 22:26–27); Cyril's ὁσιωθήσῃ ('you will be made holy') is kept. 'Light is hostile to darkness' is a paraphrase of 2 Corinthians 6:14, cited. 'The poison of asps… cursing and bitterness' follows Romans 3:13–14 word for word (itself from Psalm 140:3 = LXX 139:4 and Psalm 10:7 = LXX 9:28). 'Works of deadness' may echo the 'dead works' of Hebrews 6:1/9:14; too loose to cite. The last phrase δόξαν… τὴν δι|εστραμμένην is split across §9/§10; the whole phrase ('a distorted opinion about God') is rendered here and §10 opens with the next clause.

title: Unclean until evening: cleansing comes through Christ
english: Cyril: …or perhaps they are also those who say, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ (1 Corinthians 15:32), and those who drag the minds of the less instructed toward the pleasures of the world. Unclean, too, and apt to defile those who touch them or come near them (by the law, I mean, of shared disposition) are those of whom the most wise Paul also said somewhere: ‘If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or a drunkard, or a robber, or greedy, or an idolater, do not even eat with such a one’ (1 Corinthians 5:11). Or would you not say that for the holy and chosen race, those who have not fallen into such evils, the most fitting thing is not to mix with those who are sick with them either?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: ‘So whoever touches these,’ he says, ‘shall be in uncleanness until evening. He shall not eat of the holy things unless he washes his body with water; and when the sun has set he shall be clean, and then he shall eat of the holy things, because it is his bread’ (Leviticus 22:6–7). Besides this he also forbids eating what has died of itself or been torn by beasts, since it is quite able to defile (Leviticus 22:8). See, then, Palladius, that the putting away of all filth and the release from the charges against us could come about in us in no other way than through Christ alone, and at the time of his coming.
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: He showed that everything before the coming of the Only-begotten was unpurified and still stained, and had no share in life, when he said, ‘He shall be unclean until evening, and he shall not eat of the holy things’ (Leviticus 22:6). Or did not Emmanuel come in the last times of the age?
Palladius: Yes, that is plain.

Cyril: And we have been given life by eating the bread that is truly holy and from heaven (John 6:32–33), that is, Christ, when the time had come to its end, as though the sun were setting and bringing the measure of time to a close in evening.
Palladius: Quite so.

Cyril: This is why the one who is defiled remains unclean until evening and has no share in the holy and life-giving food, while he waits for the time of cleansing. But once he has washed in water and the sun has set, he is clean, and he has the bread from heaven as his own. For to those who have been sanctified through water, I mean in holy baptism, it has been granted, as it were, to be blessed through Christ; and he himself is the living bread, and he again is the one who came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:51; John 6:33). That the setting of the sun would mark the time of our Savior’s coming you will see clearly from what God says about the lamb to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: ‘Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them take for themselves a sheep by households’ (Exodus 12:3); ‘and it shall be kept,’ he says, ‘from the tenth day of the month until the fourteenth, and the whole…
translator_notes: Opens with the clause after the split word διεστραμμένην (rendered whole at the end of §9). The quoted law is Leviticus 22:6–7 (LXX ἐὰν μὴ λούσηται τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ὕδατι· καὶ δύῃ ὁ ἥλιος…ὅτι ἄρτος αὐτοῦ ἐστιν), and the ban on carcass and beast-torn flesh is Leviticus 22:8. 'Let us eat and drink…' is cited at 1 Corinthians 15:32 (Paul quoting Isaiah 22:13). 1 Corinthians 5:11 is quoted without Paul's 'reviler' (λοίδορος). κατά γε τὸν διαθέσεως νόμον rendered 'by the law of shared disposition': Cyril means the moral rule by which attitudes pass between companions, not the Mosaic law. μὴ γεγονόσι τὰ τοιάδε τῶν κακῶν is compressed Greek; rendered 'who have kept clear of such evils'. 'Holy and chosen race' may echo 1 Peter 2:9; not cited. ῥύπου παντὸς ἀπόθεσιν may echo 1 Peter 3:21 (σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου); not cited. 'In the last times of the age' resembles Hebrews 9:26 and 1 Peter 1:20 but is not a quotation; not cited. ἱεροφάντης rendered 'the revealer of sacred things'. The Exodus 12 quotation runs on into §11: its first clause is cited here (Exodus 12:3) and the close in §11 (Exodus 12:6); this section ends mid-sentence at πᾶν τὸ, rendered 'and the whole…'.

title: Dead flesh, torn flesh, and who may eat the holy bread
english: Cyril: …assembly of the sons of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening’ (Exodus 12:6). For the hour at which Emmanuel appeared to us is said to be the tenth, close now to evening itself, that is, to the end of the present age. What has died of itself and what has been torn by beasts bring defilement, in the spiritual sense, on those who touch them no less than leprosy does. For what has died of itself plainly signifies what is wholly dead and gone cold, as in the works that belong to the flesh, and what is torn by beasts signifies the soul that has fallen under the devil. And it is a saving thing to keep away from a man who has set his mind on dead things and gone cold in his thinking, and who, as it were, makes himself food for Satan, for Satan devours whatever souls he chooses (1 Peter 5:8). How could this fail to be clear to those who are truly sound of mind and have earnestly striven to keep as far as possible from everything that usually defiles?
Palladius: That is so.

Cyril: Since our account has now come to this point of precision, and the aim of the law is that the right to share in the holy and life-giving foods should belong not at all to the defiled, but to those who are blameless, he at once draws a careful line between the classes. He has defined who would be worthy of the blessing and able to press on toward it, and he makes clear who ought to be driven away from the sacred food, saying: ‘And no foreigner shall eat holy things; a sojourner with a priest or a hired servant shall not eat holy things. But if a priest acquires a person bought with silver, he shall eat of his bread, and those born in his house, they too shall eat of his bread’ (Leviticus 22:10–11). He shuts out the foreigner, the man of another race, as defiled and still unwashed, that is, the one who has not yet believed and does not know the true God. For how could those who cannot be bound through a spiritual and inward kinship to Christ, the great and true Priest, share in his bread? For we will not give what is holy to the dogs, and no one would throw the spiritual pearls before swine, according to the Savior’s own words (Matthew 7:6). So the foreigner has no share at all. With him he joins the sojourner and the hired servant. These again, in my own view, would be those who live for the world and conduct their lives by it, and have made the earth their homeland, as it were, by minding only the things of the flesh; but in their love for Christ they are only sojourners, living, as it were, in bare faith alone. As far as words go, they are good and reasonable, but in the deeds and ways of true piety they have strayed very far indeed. The hired servants, in turn, would perhaps be those who chose even the bare act of believing not out of reverence for the truth, but hunting for the favor of certain people as a kind of wage for seeming to be Christians; who fawn to win the attentions of those able to benefit them; who make godliness a means of gain (1 Timothy 6:5) and a cover for love of profit, and put on fair words like a mask. As far, then, as the force of the law goes…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation: §10 ends πᾶν τὸ, §11 begins πλῆθος τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ πρὸς ἑσπέραν, so the turn starts '…assembly of the sons of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening’'. The quotation is Exodus 12:3 (take a sheep by households) and 12:6 (kept until the fourteenth; the whole assembly slaughters it toward evening), abridged; LXX has πλῆθος συναγωγῆς, which the English renders 'assembly'. 'The tenth is said to be the hour': Cyril turns the tenth day of Exodus 12:3 into a late hour of the world's day; no Gospel text is quoted, so no citation. 'Satan devours whatever souls he chooses' is a clear allusion to 1 Peter 5:8, cited. Leviticus 22:10–11 LXX (ἔγκτητον ἀργυρίου; Migne prints ἔκκτητον). 'Minding only the things of the flesh' echoes Romans 8:5 and 'living for the world' may echo Colossians 2:20; left uncited as loose wording. 'The great and true Priest' recalls Hebrews 4:14 but is a title, not a quotation; uncited. 'Make godliness a means of gain' is 1 Timothy 6:5 (πορισμὸν εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν), cited. Doubtful syntax: ἐν ψιλῇ δὲ ὥσπερ καὶ μόνῃ παροικοῦντες τῇ πίστει, τὴν εἰς Χριστὸν ἀγάπησιν; the accusative is taken as 'in respect of their love for Christ'. The section ends mid-sentence (ὅσον μὲν οὖν ἧκεν εἰς νόμου δύναμιν), rendered 'As far, then, as the force of the law goes…'; the sentence finishes in §12. The opening citation is Exodus 12:6, since Exodus 12:3 is cited beside its clause in §10.

title: The priest’s household and the priest’s daughter
english: Cyril: …if the sojourners and the hired servants are ranked with the foreigners, they will also be with them, as far as possible from the holy things; and since they are all but sick with kindred faults, they will justly suffer a penalty of the same kind. But he said that the sharing of the holy things must be left open to the members of the household. For those born in the priests’ households will eat, he says, and anyone they may happen to buy. By ‘acquired’, ‘bought with silver’ and ‘born in the house’ he means, I take it, the one who is genuine in faith, a member of the household in spirit, and bought with a price, as the blessed Paul says (1 Corinthians 6:20). For, as it is written, ‘Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us’ (Galatians 3:13).
Palladius: True.

Cyril: He further commands that if the daughter of a priest is married to a foreign man, she shall not eat of the firstfruits of the holy things (Leviticus 22:12). He has plainly honored the member of the household by allowing him to share in the holy things as one who is genuine. Yet those who have this close bond with the priest must firmly refuse to cling to people who are not their own by faith or by way of life and have not gained through virtue a kind of kinship with them; this will be clear enough to anyone willing to search the evidence of the sacred Scriptures. For just as in the passages already read he made the leper unclean, and with him the man with a discharge, and made the one who came near them, joined to them, as it were, by touch, a sharer in their defilement and uncleanness, so here too he says that the priest’s daughter, even if she happens to have a holy kinship, will gain nothing from it when she is joined to another, that is, to a foreigner, one who is in no way akin to her and not of the blood of Israel. Let this, then, be the historical sense. But when we carry the law over into spiritual contemplation, we say that by the priest’s daughter he means the soul that has been born again of water and the Spirit (John 3:5) by the power of Christ, and called through faith to sanctification. Yet even such a soul, he says, may have no share in the holy things if she is married to a foreign man, that is, if she joins herself to people who are not truly holy and have no spiritual bond with God. For bodies the manner of union would be bodily, but for spirits it is spiritual.
Palladius: And who, would we say, have been carried away into this?

Cyril: Those whom the solemn word of Wisdom sought to keep safe when it said: ‘My son, do not let ungodly men lead you astray, and do not consent if they urge you, saying: Come with us, share in blood’ (Proverbs 1:10–11). We will also add those who in their ignorance have turned away from the right faith and run after the flesh; who do not admit the words given through the Holy Spirit, but have given heed to spirits of error, through the hypocrisy of liars who are seared in their minds (1 Timothy 4:1–2). These have thrust aside their close bond with Christ, and in truth they have been married to foreign men; they have accepted the devil’s seed, and in error they bear as fruit the…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, finishing §11's 'As far, then, as the force of the law goes…'. μόνον δὲ οὐχί is taken as 'all but' (they are all but sick with kindred faults). ἀνεῖσθαι rendered 'left open'. The household-and-purchase terms (ἔκκτητον, ἀργυρώνητον, οἰκογενῆ) gloss Leviticus 22:11, cited in §11. 'Bought with a price, as blessed Paul says' = 1 Corinthians 6:20 (also 7:23). 'Married to a foreign man' renders the idiom γίνεσθαι ἀνδρί (Leviticus 22:12, LXX θυγάτηρ ἀνθρώπου ἱερέως ἐὰν γένηται ἀνδρὶ ἀλλογενεῖ…οὐ φάγεται); the same idiom returns at the end (γεγόνασι… ἀνθρώποις ἀλλογενέσι), so it is rendered the same way there. πολυπραγμονεῖν τῶν ἱερῶν Γραμμάτων τὴν πίστιν: πίστις here taken as 'evidence' or 'proof' of Scripture, not personal faith. οἰκεῖον ἐν πνεύματι kept lowercase ('in spirit') as the contrast with blood kinship; in ἐξ ὕδατός τε καὶ πνεύματος (John 3:5) Spirit is capitalized. Proverbs 1:10–11 LXX; Cyril stops before the rest of verse 11 (κρύψωμεν δὲ εἰς γῆν ἄνδρα δίκαιον ἀδίκως). The phrase on false teachers follows 1 Timothy 4:1–2 closely, except that Cyril writes 'seared in their mind' (τὸν νοῦν) where Paul has 'conscience'; cited. Uncited loose echoes: 'run after the flesh' (2 Peter 2:10; Jude 7), 'devil's seed' (the tares, Matthew 13:25, 39), the body/spirit union contrast (1 Corinthians 6:16–17), 'called to sanctification' (1 Thessalonians 4:7). The section ends mid-phrase: καρποφοροῦντες ἐν πλάνῃ τὰ πλάνης | ἔργα καὶ ἀπωλείας (§13), so the English stops at 'in error they bear as fruit the…' and §13 continues '…works of error and of destruction'. Τὴν πρὸς αὐτὸν οἰκειότητα rendered 'close bond with the priest' (αὐτόν = the priest of the law, read as Christ, as in §11 and at the end of §12); διησφαλίζετο means Wisdom sought to keep these people safe, not that it guarded against them.

title: The priest’s widowed daughter: the soul that returns, and the Synagogue that strayed
english: Cyril: …works of error and of destruction. So a soul is to be cast off, even if it was once sacred and holy, when it has been caught in such shameful defilements. For whatever becomes loathsome and defiled through attaching itself to base and unholy men is altogether unholy. Right after this he laid down another law, close to the first; it runs as follows: ‘And if a priest’s daughter becomes a widow, cast out, and has no offspring, she shall return to her father’s house as in her youth; she shall eat of her father’s bread’ (Leviticus 22:13). The historical sense, I think, is plain; but we must go on to the inner and hidden meanings. For if, he says, a soul should be cast off as condemned, and is seen from then on to be without a husband, that is, without the spiritual Bridegroom, and bears no fruit of virtue, let her hurry her steps back to what she was at the beginning, and let her return quickly to her own father’s house, seeking, that is, through repentance, to belong to God; and then she will eat of his bread. Nothing prevents us from applying the force of these words also to those we spoke of a moment ago. For if, he says, a sacred and holy soul, carried away by profane men, should slip into error and take in the defilement of alien doctrines, and so become like a widow, sent away from God, but should then somehow come to her senses and learn what she has slipped into, let her return to the Father. For he receives those who have strayed, if they prove clean of the unholy seeds sown in them, and if they carry no trace of the foulness of those who led them astray; and so he gathers them into one flock with the holy worshipers, setting himself before them as bread from heaven, their life-giving food (John 6:32–33). And I think the lawgiver also hints at something else to us through these laws. For he foretells, as it were, the falling away of the Synagogue of the Jews, the punishment that follows it, and the kindness that will be shown to her in due time, which by the mercy of God brings her back and restores her to what she was at the beginning. For ‘a priest’s daughter,’ he says, ‘if she is married to a man of another race, shall not eat of the firstfruits of the holy things’ (Leviticus 22:12). For as far as teaching and instruction go, the inspired Moses became a kind of father to the Synagogue of the Jews. She was, then, a priest’s daughter; for Moses too was a minister of sacred rites, since he was of the blood and tribe of Levi. But this man’s daughter became the wife of a man of another race. For she held what God had laid down to be worth almost nothing, and, in a manner of speaking, disregarded the seeds from above; she has studied teachings that are the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9; Isaiah 29:13), and she bears fruit for the opinions of others. That is why God reproached her, saying to her through the voice of Jeremiah: ‘Lift up your eyes and look straight ahead, and see: where have you not defiled yourself? By the roadsides you sat waiting for them like a lonely crow, and you defiled the land with your prostitution and your wickedness; and you had many shepherds, to your own stumbling’ (Jeremiah 3:2–3). These, however, are the ancient charges against the Synagogue of the Jews; and akin to them are also…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence: 'ἔργα καὶ ἀπωλείας' completes s.12's 'καρποφοροῦντες ἐν πλάνῃ τὰ πλάνης' (bearing in error the works of error and of destruction). Lev 22:13: Cyril's text reads 'χήρα ἐκβεβλημένη' (widow, cast out) without the LXX's 'ἤ' (widow or divorced); rendered as he has it. The Migne print capitalises 'Πατρὸς' inside the first Lev 22:13 quotation; the literal referent is the woman's father, so lowercase in the quotation. 'νοητοῦ νυμφίου' rendered 'spiritual Bridegroom' (Christ). 'οἰκείωσιν πρὸς Θεόν' rendered 'to belong to God'. In 'Δέχεται … παρατιθεὶς ἑαυτὸν ὡς ἄρτον' the subject slides from the Father to Christ as the bread; English keeps the unspecified 'he'. 'Bread from heaven … life-giving' cited to John 6:32–33 (6:33: the bread of God gives life to the world). 'θεσπέσιος' rendered 'inspired'. Moses' Levitical descent (Exodus 2:1; 6:16–20) is stated as fact, not quoted; uncited. 'διδασκαλίας, ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων' is the wording of Isaiah 29:13 LXX as quoted in Matthew 15:9. Jeremiah 3:2–3 follows the LXX: 'ἐξεφύρθης' (literally 'mixed/fouled yourself'), 'deserted crow' (Hebrew: an Arab in the wilderness), and 'you had many shepherds' (Hebrew 3:3 differs: showers withheld). Section ends mid-sentence; s.14 continues with 'new' charges. s.12's English ends 'bear as fruit the…' (Greek τὰ πλάνης ends s.12), so s.13 opens '…works of error and of destruction' and the joined phrase reads whole.

title: The Synagogue will return to the Father; holy things eaten in ignorance
english: Cyril: …new charges, those that concern Christ himself. For she utterly refuses the Bridegroom who comes from above, from God the Father, and gives heed to the words of the scribes and Pharisees. So she has become the wife of a man of another race, and for that reason she has remained without a share in the holy things; for she did not eat the bread from heaven, that is, Christ (John 6:32). You see the charges, and the punishment that Christ at once brought on those guilty of such impiety. Now observe also how they have been shown mercy and been brought back to what they were at the beginning. ‘A priest’s daughter,’ he says, ‘if she becomes a widow, cast out, and there is no offspring in her, shall return to her father’s house as in her youth, and shall eat of her father’s bread’ (Leviticus 22:13). For the Synagogue of the Jews was shown to be a widow and cast out because of her impiety toward Christ; she has remained in sins, possessing none of the spiritual goods, and has continued so for a long time. But she will return to her father’s house; for she too will be called to God through faith; with us she will claim as Father the Creator of all things, and so would come to share in the blessing of Christ. The prophet’s words will make this mystery clear to you as well; for he spoke thus: ‘For the sons of Israel will remain many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or oracles; and afterward the sons of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God and their king, and they will be filled with awe at the Lord and at his good things in the last days’ (Hosea 3:4–5).
Palladius: What you say is true.

Cyril: So the sacred things, that is, the holy things, are fit to be eaten and shared by those who, as far as it rests with themselves, are without blemish. But they will no longer be set before those who are not sound, or who have been defiled by their ties with others. For it is written: ‘With the crooked you will deal crookedly’ (Psalm 18:26). He made it plain at once that even for those who are truly consecrated it is not without penalty to treat the holy things as if they were for common use, and to think they differ in no way from other things; for he says: ‘And a man who eats the holy things in ignorance shall add a fifth more to it and give the holy thing to the priest; and he shall not profane the holy things of the sons of Israel which they set apart for the Lord, and they will bring on themselves the iniquity of trespass when they eat their holy things; for I am the Lord who sanctifies them’ (Leviticus 22:14–16).
Palladius: I do not quite understand what you mean.

Cyril: You will learn it very clearly; there is nothing hard about it. The offerings dedicated for a pleasing aroma, a calf, say, or a sheep, were carried up to the altar in part, once the entrails, the feet and head, the fat, and sometimes the kidneys too had been taken out; and with what remained they fed the priests. For ‘those who eat the sacrifices are partners in the altar’ (1 Corinthians 10:18), as the…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing s.13's 'ἀδελφὰ δὲ τούτοις καὶ / νέα'. Lev 22:13 again read with Cyril's 'χήρα ἐκβεβλημένη' and here 'σπέρμα … ἐν αὐτῇ'. Hosea 3:4–5 quoted from the LXX but without 'David' before 'their king' (LXX and Hebrew both have it); 'δήλων' is the LXX word for the Urim-type oracle (cf. Exodus 28:30 LXX δήλωσις), rendered 'oracles'; Hebrew has 'pillar … ephod or teraphim'. 'ἐκστήσονται' rendered 'filled with awe' (Hebrew: 'come trembling'). 'Μετὰ στρεβλοῦ διαστρέψεις' is LXX Psalm 17:27 = English Psalm 18:26 (also 2 Samuel 22:27); LXX sense 'with the crooked you will twist/deal crookedly'. Lev 22:14–16: Cyril reads 'οὐ βεβηλώσει' (he shall not profane) where the LXX has the plural; rendered as he has it; 'ἐπάξουσιν … ἀνομίαν πλημμελείας' kept close to the LXX. In 'ἐξαιρουμένων τῶν ἐντοσθίων …' Cyril does not say whether the parts taken out are those burned or those set aside; English keeps the same ambiguity. 'Pleasing aroma' (ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας) is the standing Levitical formula, uncited. Section ends mid-word ('ὁ θε-'); s.15 completes 'inspired Paul said'.

title: Eli’s sons, the added fifth, and priests kept from the dead
english: Cyril: …inspired Paul said. So it was necessary that the portion of what was brought be consecrated to God, according to the law that fitted each offering, and that the ministers be sustained with the rest of the body of the sacrifice. But if anyone kept back the whole gift entirely for himself and spent it on his own needs, having burned none of it, he was charged under the law as one who had eaten holy things. This is just what the sons of Eli the priest did: they seized and profaned the sacred offerings before the sacrifices were made, and said most impiously to those who came to sacrifice, ‘Give meat for the priest to roast’ (1 Samuel 2:15). But those deeds, being deliberate and plainly insolent, were punished accordingly. ‘But if,’ he says, ‘someone, either overtaken by forgetfulness or not knowing exactly what the laws require, should do any such thing, let him bear a penalty: let him repay the same amount without fail, and let him add to it a fifth as well,’ that is, the fifth part of the value; ‘for in this way he will be cleared of the charges and will ward off the harm that comes from ignorance’ (Leviticus 22:14; Leviticus 5:15–16). If, then, what is done in ignorance is not free from indictment, what would anyone think of what is done out of madness and audacity? Those, then, who have the care of the sacred things must refrain from seeking to claim anything for themselves before the sacrifice; otherwise let them know that, having committed grave offenses, they will incur punishment and come under the wrath of God. Or do you say that this is not true, my friend?
Palladius: It is entirely true.

Cyril: He made it clear that those who serve as priests must be holy and washed clean, and must shake off with all their strength any frame of mind that is in some way dead and cold, and not alive to virtue; for he says: ‘Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them: They shall not be defiled for the dead among their people, except for the nearest of their household: for father and mother, for sons and daughters, for a brother, and for a virgin sister who is close to him and has not been given to a husband; for these he may be defiled. He shall not be defiled suddenly among his people, so as to profane himself. And you shall not shave a bald patch on your heads for the dead, and they shall not shave the beard from their faces, nor cut gashes in their flesh. They shall be holy to their God, and they shall not profane the name of their God; for they offer the sacrifices of the Lord, the gifts of their God, and they shall be holy’ (Leviticus 21:1–6). For if one looks closely into the truth of the matter, another man’s death would bring no defilement at all on anyone. Bodily deadness, however, may be a type of the deadness that is inward and in souls, by which anyone who comes near it must be defiled, whether by consenting to it or by doing the same deeds. For it would befit the saints to keep away from dead works and to stay as far from them as they can, and it is good not to keep company with those who are sick with such things. For it is written: ‘Whoever touches pitch…
translator_notes: Opens mid-word, completing s.14's 'ὁ θε-/σπέσιος Παῦλος' (1 Corinthians 10:18 is cited in s.14 beside the quotation). 'τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ προσκομισθέντος' read as 'τὸ ἀπὸ …' (the portion of what was brought); the printed ὑπό gives no sense here. 'Give meat for the priest to roast' is 1 Samuel 2:15 (LXX 1 Kingdoms 2:15); the whole scene is 1 Samuel 2:12–17, cited only at the quotation. The Migne quotation marks around 'But if … ignorance' enclose Cyril's own paraphrase of the law on eating holy things in ignorance (Leviticus 22:14; compare Leviticus 5:15–16), not a verbatim LXX quotation; cited to Leviticus 22:14. 'ὑπὸ θείαν … κίνησιν' (literally 'under divine movement') is Cyril's usual idiom for God's wrath; rendered 'the wrath of God'. 'Παντάπασι μὲν οὖν' answers a negatively framed question; context shows Palladius affirms the statement is true. 'Ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς' in Leviticus 21:1 LXX means 'for (dead) persons'; rendered 'for the dead'. 'ἐξάπινα' (suddenly) is the LXX reading of Leviticus 21:4 (Hebrew differs). 'Dead works' echoes the phrase of Hebrews 6:1 and 9:14 but is not quoted or argued from; left uncited. The Sirach 13:1 quotation runs across the break into s.16, where the citation stands. Cyril's paraphrase draws on Leviticus 5:15–16 LXX as well as 22:14 (λήθῃ 'forgetfulness', ἀποτείσαι 'repay', the added fifth, release from guilty liability), so both are cited, after the whole paraphrase.

title: Mourning kept within measure, and the laws on a priest’s marriage
english: Cyril: …will be defiled’ (Sirach 13:1). For whoever does not refuse to cling to another would very easily share in his wickedness. Yet the law allows the consecrated to incur defilement without blame for father and mother, for children and brothers, and indeed for close kin, by going even to their lifeless bodies, out of reverence for nature; and in this it overlooks wrongs that are wrongs only as types, so that those who are known to God might not seem hard, haughty and unfeeling; and indeed the law says plainly: ‘Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you’ (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16). In another way too, and for another reason, we say the consecrated are barred from mourning. For they are priests of life, and offer the sacred gifts to God for the undoing of death (for the death of Christ, foreshadowed through sheep and calves, is the undoing of death); how then would it be fitting for them to be weighed down with grief over death? So too the inspired Paul writes plainly to those baptized into Christ in the hope of life and resurrection: ‘I say this so that you may not grieve as the rest do who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus, and will raise them with us’ (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). The law, then, allowed the consecrated to go to those of their very closest kin who had died. But it sets a measure on the matter, and does not let them undo what most befits them by going to excess, beyond what is needed, so that the revered dignity of the priesthood may not be wronged. For it keeps them from baring their heads as others do, and from shaving off the beard to the disgrace of the face; and it commands them not even to entertain the thought of the impious acts of pagan frenzy, I mean the gashes cut into the flesh (Leviticus 21:5). For there is nothing unreasonable in sharing the grief of one’s own family; but to lose all decorum would be unseemly and quite senseless. ‘For let all things,’ he says, ‘be done decently and in order’ (1 Corinthians 14:40). And the Savior himself has commanded us as well that the things of God must be honored above even duties to parents, as the old law required of the priests; for he says: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:37).
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: He commands, then, that the priests be defiled over the dead as little as possible. And showing us in other ways too that the holy cannot be joined or blended with the profane, he laid down for us the laws on marriage, adding at once: ‘As for every priest: they shall not take a wife who is a prostitute or profaned, and they shall not take a woman put away by her husband; for he is holy to the Lord his God, and you shall sanctify him; he offers the gifts of the Lord your God; he shall be holy, for I the Lord who sanctify them am holy’ (Leviticus 21:7–8). Now the woman who has truly lived as a prostitute and been defiled is sick, clothed with the charge of shameful deeds, and has an undisputed…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation, completing s.15's 'Ὁ ἁπτόμενος πίσσης / μολυνθήσεται' (Sirach 13:1). 'τῶν εἰς τύπον ἀλογήσας ἀδικημάτων' (literally 'having disregarded the wrongs [reckoned] for a type') is rendered 'set aside wrongs that are wrongs only as a type': in these cases the law overlooks the symbolic defilement; the aorist participle is masculine singular and seems to have the law (or lawgiver) as subject. 'καί τοι' taken as 'and indeed', supporting the concession. 'Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you' matches both Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16 LXX; both cited. 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14 is quoted freely: 'Τοῦτο δὲ λέγω' replaces Paul's 'We do not want you to be uninformed', and 'καὶ ἐγερεῖ σὺν ἡμῖν' (and will raise them with us) is not in 1 Thessalonians 4:14 (compare 2 Corinthians 4:14); rendered as Cyril has it. 'μανίας Ἑλληνικῆς' rendered 'pagan frenzy' (Cyril's 'Hellenes' = pagans); the reference is to Leviticus 21:5, quoted in s.15, so cited again here. The sentence 'Προτετιμηκότας δὲ τὰ Θεοῦ· καὶ τῶν εἰς γονέας αὐτοὺς … ἡγεῖσθαι προστέταχεν' is grammatically loose (punctuation in the print splits it); taken as: the Savior has commanded that the things of God take precedence over duties to parents, which the old law also required of priests. 'ἀγαπῶν' for Matthew's 'φιλῶν' is Cyril's wording. 'Ἥκιστα … καταμιαίνεσθαι' rendered 'as little as possible', since the law has just allowed defilement for near kin ('least of all' would contradict that). 'ἀσυμφανές' (literally 'not appearing together') may be a misprint for 'ἀσυμφυές' (not growing together); rendered 'cannot be … blended'. Leviticus 21:7–8 follows the LXX; 'Ἐπὶ παντὸς ἱερέως' (as for every priest) is Cyril's lead-in. Section ends mid-sentence; s.17 completes '…condemnation'. 'Προτετιμηκότας … αὐτοὺς … ἡμῖν ὁ Σωτὴρ ἡγεῖσθαι προστέταχεν' is loose; ἡγεῖσθαι taken as 'take precedence', αὐτούς as the priests under the old law, ἡμῖν as the Savior's command to us; English reordered to put the main verb first.

title: The unfaithful Synagogue, and the law for the high priest
english: Cyril: …condemnation. Yet the woman cast out by her husband is by no means free of blame either, for she would not be driven from her husband’s home without some cause. Those who have been brought into so holy a ministry, then, must keep away not only from evils whose guilt is plain and open to view, but also, I think, from anything that might bring with it a name for wickedness, a poor opinion of them, or the indecency of lying under a great many suspicions. The passage also seems to hint at the misfortune of the Synagogue of the Jews. Because she played the harlot with many shepherds, as it is written (Jeremiah 3:1), Christ did not receive her into spiritual fellowship: Christ the wholly pure priest, who offers himself to the Father for us as a choice gift, who is holy with us in his humanity, although he himself sanctifies the whole creation, since he is God from God. He made the mystery plainer still when he said: ‘And if the daughter of a priest profanes herself by playing the harlot, she profanes the name of her father; she shall be burned with fire.’ (Leviticus 21:9) For the Synagogue of the Jews has been given over to the flame as unholy and profane, because she followed the opinions of the scribes and Pharisees and devoted her whole mind to the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9). So it was very just that she heard the prophet say: ‘How have you become a harlot, faithful city of Zion, full of justice?’ (Isaiah 1:21) Having played the harlot, then, and utterly disregarded the spiritual Bridegroom from above, she has become fuel for the fire. So the prophet Jeremiah too sheds bitter tears over her and says: ‘A beautiful olive tree, well shaded in appearance: so the Lord called your name. At the sound of its circumcision a fire was kindled against it; great is the affliction upon you. Its branches have become useless, and the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has pronounced evil against you.’ (Jeremiah 11:16–17) To turn away from what is right, then, and to seek to attach oneself to shameful and unholy teachers, is a form of spiritual harlotry.
Palladius: That is my view too.

Cyril: In what has been said, the types are rather faint and not very clear in the case of the other priests, but in Aaron, who bears the image of Christ, they shine out, as it were. For he said again: ‘And the priest who is great among his brothers, on whose head the anointing oil has been poured, and who has been consecrated to put on the garments, shall not take the turban from his head’—that is, shall not take off the mitre—‘and shall not tear his garments. He shall not go in to any dead person; he shall not be defiled for his father or for his mother. He shall not go out of the holy place, and shall not profane what is consecrated to his God, because the holy anointing oil of God is upon him. I am the Lord.’ (Leviticus 21:10–12) ‘He shall take as his wife a virgin of his own kindred. A widow, a woman cast out, a woman profaned, or a harlot, these he shall not take; but he shall take as his wife only a virgin from his own people. And he shall not profane his offspring among his people.’ (Leviticus 21:13–15)
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence: s.16 ends 'καὶ ἀναμφίλογον' and this section opens 'ἔχει τὴν κατάῤῥησιν', so the joined English reads '…and has an undisputed… condemnation.' 'Many shepherds' is the LXX of Jeremiah 3:1 (Hebrew 'many lovers'). 'Commandments of men' cited to Matthew 15:9 (from Isaiah 29:13 LXX; compare Colossians 2:22). 'Offers himself to the Father as a choice gift' echoes Ephesians 5:2 in thought but not wording; left uncited. Jeremiah 11:16–17 LXX: 'circumcision' (περιτομή, in the LXX the lopping of the tree) kept because Cyril reads it of the Jews; 'Lord of hosts' renders Κύριος τῶν δυνάμεων. Leviticus 21:10–15 LXX: ἀποκιδαρώσει rendered 'take the turban from', Cyril's gloss ἀπομιτρώσει 'take off the mitre' (he distinguishes the two in section 18). The Leviticus quotation runs on into section 18 (verse 15 ends there).

title: A priesthood and kingship never laid aside; the Life does not mourn the dead
english: Cyril: …‘I am the Lord God, who sanctifies them.’ (Leviticus 21:15) You see plainly how Emmanuel, the Christ, is named here, still in types, in the person of Aaron. For he who is himself the priest perfect in every way was anointed with the Spirit, according to the Scriptures (Acts 10:38). So the glory of his priesthood is one he can never lose. For ‘he shall not take the turban,’ it says, ‘from his head’ (Leviticus 21:10); that is, he will not lay aside the dress that befits a priest. For it was said to the Savior and Redeemer of all: ‘You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.’ (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:17) ‘The former priests were many in number, because death prevented them from continuing; but he, because he remains for ever, holds his priesthood permanently. Therefore he is also able to save completely those who draw near to God through him.’ (Hebrews 7:23–25) This is what the inspired Paul wrote. So the fact that the turban is never taken from his head would hint that his priesthood can never be lost. And if the reading were ‘He shall not take the mitre from his head,’ you will readily understand that his kingship is perpetual and cannot be shaken; for the mitre, with the golden band across the front of the brow, would be a symbol of rule and kingship. ‘Nor shall he tear his garments,’ it says (Leviticus 21:10). Some people are in the habit of doing this over the dead, but such a thing is wholly foreign to Christ. For the Life would be the last to suffer grief at a death. The Life has nothing at all to do with what is dead; rather, it is itself the undoing of death and the overthrow of corruption. So the Savior once rebuked those who wanted to wail over the little daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, saying: ‘Go away, and do not weep, for the girl is not dead but asleep.’ (Matthew 9:24; Luke 8:52) For it was truly out of place for them to shed tears as over a dead girl when the Life of all, that is, Christ, was present. And if he wept over Lazarus (John 11:35), we say that this was the fruit of his tender love, and the compassion that divine gentleness has toward us. For our nature, under the tyranny of death, was being pitied, and his tear was its release from that suffering.
Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: That there is nothing profane in Christ in any way is hinted at indirectly when the law says that the high priest must keep away from what is dead, going near no dead person at all, even though this means setting aside the honor owed to father, mother and brothers. See how wise the law is, and how seriously it takes the good order that befits what it signifies. In the case of the other priests it made allowance for nature, and for the dead who were very close and of their own blood it allowed the consecrated to carry out the customary rites without blame (Leviticus 21:1–3). It was not greatly concerned there about a fault against the shadow. For in that case the charges were written with us in view, and the type pointed to human beings; and if some defilement should attach to them, there is nothing strange in that. ‘For we all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2), and in us our nature has fallen sick with wrongdoing. But in the case of the great high priest, that is, Christ,…
translator_notes: Opens with the end of the Leviticus 21:10–15 quotation begun in section 17. 'Named … as in Aaron' (ὠνομασμένον) likely plays on 'the anointing oil' (ἔλαιον τὸ χριστόν), Aaron as the anointed one; kept literal. 'Anointed with the Spirit' cited to Acts 10:38 (same verb and noun; compare Isaiah 61:1, Luke 4:18). Psalm 110:4 is LXX Psalm 109:4, quoted in Hebrews 7:17; Cyril runs it straight into Hebrews 7:23–25 and assigns both to Paul. Matthew 9:24 gives 'Go away … not dead but asleep', Luke 8:52 gives 'do not weep'; Cyril combines them. 'The Life' is capitalised as a title of Christ. 'Brothers' in the list of kin is Cyril's own addition (Leviticus 21:11 names only father and mother; 21:2 lists brother for ordinary priests). 'Great high priest' (ἀρχιερεὺς ὁ μέγας) may echo Hebrews 4:14 but also renders Leviticus 21:10 'the great priest'; left uncited. The section ends mid-sentence; the clause completes in section 19.

title: Christ free of all profanation; the virgin bride; no steps to the altar
english: Cyril: …reverence has been kept pure even in the type itself, and the shadows have been kept free of anything counterfeit, so that the beauty of the truth should not be misrepresented, as though it had suffered harm in them. For Christ is free of all profanation; he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21) and is beyond all defilement, or rather, he is all radiance and spiritual purity. He remains within all holiness, even if, here at least, its brightness has grown faint, because he stands firm on the laws of his own nature and is always the same and unchanging. This, I think, is what is meant by ‘He shall not go out of the holy place, and shall not profane what is consecrated to his God.’ (Leviticus 21:12) He says very rightly that he must take a virgin as his wife into the fellowship of marriage (Leviticus 21:13–14), and he declares the woman who has been driven out unfit for him. She may also stand as a type of the Synagogue of the Jews, for she has been cast out of union with him, and he says of her through the prophet’s voice: ‘She is not my wife, and I am not her husband.’ (Hosea 2:2) But Paul betrothed the Church from the Gentiles to Christ as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2), without spot or wrinkle, or rather holy and blameless (Ephesians 5:27). Taken in this way, of the Church from the Gentiles and of the mother of the Jews, the riddle would be true and the type not without beauty. But if someone wishes to apply the force of these ideas fittingly to each individual, we say that Christ has no union with profane and unholy souls; but with souls that are wholly chaste and pure, like virgins, he is joined spiritually, makes them fruitful, and calls them his own kin. For ‘whoever does the will of my Father in heaven,’ he says, ‘is my brother and my sister and my mother.’ (Matthew 12:50)
Palladius: You have put it rightly.

Cyril: He has plainly set out in his oracles what sort of men those chosen for sacred service must be, what they should rightly be eager to do, and what they ought to be free of. But it was surely wise, besides this, to state openly how they must perform the sacred rites, and to regulate by laws the kinds of sacrifices and everything that is offered, so that the whole matter might be blameless for them and they might in this way make their ministry most pleasing.
