So first of all he says: ‘You shall not go up by steps to my altar, so that you may not uncover your nakedness on it.’ (Exodus 20:26) But someone will say at once: how could this happen, when he gave the priests undergarments made of linen ‘to cover the nakedness’ of their flesh (Exodus 28:42)? Even if they had to climb up high, then, it would have done them no harm, since their nakedness was covered. What, then, shall we say the law is aiming at? The worshippers of idols thought it glorious and even necessary to set up altars high in their temple precincts, and they gave little thought to the need to be decently covered.
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing the clause begun at the end of section 18. The printed 'κἂν εἰ ἐξίτηλον ἔχων τὸ ἔν γε τούτῳ διαφανές' makes sense as it stands and is now translated, concessive included ('even if, here at least, its brightness has grown faint'): the holiness rests on Christ's own nature, so it stays whole even where the type shows it only faintly (compare 'the types are rather faint' in section 17). The earlier emendation to ἀνεξίτηλον and the dropped κἂν εἰ are withdrawn. Still worth a glance at the PG 68 column 817 scan. 'Or rather, he is all radiance and spiritual purity' takes the genitives λαμπρότητος … καθαρότητος νοητῆς as genitives of quality; another possible reading is 'beyond … even spiritual radiance and purity'. 'Knew no sin' cited to 2 Corinthians 5:21 (τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν). Hosea 2:2 is LXX/Hebrew Hosea 2:4. 'Mother of the Jews' means the Synagogue. Exodus 20:26 is Hebrew 20:23 in some printed Hebrew Bibles; Exodus 28:42 is 28:38 in some LXX editions. 'Temple precincts' renders τεμένεσιν.

title: Humility at the altar, and the fire that never goes out
english: Cyril: So the law wisely takes what usually happened among them as a starting point to raise the divine ministers to something better, and leads them, as it were from a bodily type, to spiritual contemplation. For ‘you shall not go up by steps to my altar,’ it says, ‘so that you may not uncover your nakedness on it.’ (Exodus 20:26) That is: Let the divine minister who has been consecrated for my service seek what is lowly and not leap up to the heights. Let him renounce boastfulness, so that he may not be seen as shameful and unlovely. For arrogance is utterly unlovely and shameful, and a most grievous sickness of the mind. ‘The greater you are,’ it says, ‘the more you must humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord.’ (Sirach 3:18) And the Savior’s disciple also writes: ‘Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation.’ (James 1:9–10) For the rich man will pass away like the grass and will differ in no way from the flowers of the field (James 1:10–11).
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: So he said that the minister must be free of pride and disdain. And how he may perform his sacred service in the most lawful and irreproachable way you will learn with full clarity, for it is written in Leviticus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the whole burnt offering. The whole burnt offering shall stay burning on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn on it; it shall not be put out. The priest shall put on a linen tunic, and he shall put linen undergarments on his body; and he shall take away from the altar the burnt portion of the whole burnt offering, which the fire has consumed, and set it beside the altar. Then he shall take off his robe and put on another robe, and carry the burnt portion outside the camp to a clean place. And the fire on the altar shall burn on it and shall not be put out; the priest shall burn wood on it every morning, lay the whole burnt offering in order on it, and place on it the fat of the peace offering. And fire shall burn on the altar continually; it shall not be put out.’ (Leviticus 6:8–13) The fire of the altar, then, is continual and wholly unceasing; and it is not foreign or brought from outside, but its own, that is, the fire that is from above and from heaven. And what does this mean? Our holy altar is filled with the glory of God, and the divine and ineffable nature is pictured in the form of fire. But the passage also seems to hint, and very aptly, at something mystical.
Palladius: What do you mean by that?

Cyril: Were we not saying that Emmanuel himself is, as in a type, the divine altar, through whom we draw near to God the Father, offering spiritual worship and all but sacrificing the fragrance of the virtues and the holiness of the gospel way of life? For ‘present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual worship.’ (Romans 12:1)
translator_notes: Leviticus 6:8–13 in English Bibles is Leviticus 6:1–6 in the LXX and Hebrew. κατακάρπωσις rendered 'burnt portion' (what the fire has consumed); τὸ στέαρ τοῦ σωτηρίου rendered 'the fat of the peace offering' (LXX 'of the deliverance/salvation offering'). Sirach 3:18 numbering is the same in Rahlfs and NRSV. 'Pass away like the grass … flowers of the field' is Cyril's paraphrase of James 1:10–11 (compare Isaiah 40:6–7), cited as a clear allusion. λογικῶς / λογικὴ λατρεία rendered 'spiritual worship' both times, so the echo of Romans 12:1 stays visible (also 'reasonable/rational'). 'Fire from above and from heaven' may recall Leviticus 9:24 and 'the divine nature pictured as fire' may recall Deuteronomy 4:24 / Hebrews 12:29; neither is quoted, so neither is cited. 'Were we not saying' points back to an earlier book where Emmanuel is read as the altar. 'Draw near to God' (προσίεμεν) echoes Hebrews 7:25 loosely; left uncited.

title: The altar fire that never goes out: the Spirit remaining on Christ
english: Palladius: We did say so; I will keep it in mind.

Cyril: Consider, then, that the law does not allow the fire that came down from heaven upon the altar to die down, or, as it were, to fade and go away, but has it stay on the altar always and make its home there without ceasing (Leviticus 6:12–13). And John the Baptist bore witness about Christ: ‘I have seen the Spirit descending from heaven in the form of a dove, and it remained on him. And I did not know him,’ he says, ‘but he who sent me to baptize said to me: He on whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining on him, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit’ (John 1:32–33). So the Holy Spirit was being prefigured, still as in shadows, coming down upon Christ in the form of fire and always remaining on him. For the fire of the altar never sleeps and never ceases at all. That the Spirit is likened to the nature of fire, the blessed Baptist also assures you when he says to the crowds of the Jews: ‘I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie’ (John 1:26–27). And he said: ‘He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire’ (Matthew 3:11). For we have been baptized not into fire that the senses perceive, but in the Holy Spirit, who like fire melts away the defilement in souls. That is why it is also written of Christ: ‘Behold, he comes in like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap; and he will sit refining and cleansing, as silver and as gold’ (Malachi 3:2–3). The fire of the altar, then, cannot be quenched. For the Holy Spirit has remained in Christ, even though the Spirit is in him by nature, inasmuch as he is God and is understood to be God. The law also called the fire the altar’s own (Leviticus 6:9). For even though the Only-begotten became man, and in the manner fitting for humanity is also said to have come to share in the Spirit, the Spirit is nonetheless both his and in him, and truly his own. But if someone chooses to apply this passage to each of those sanctified through faith in Christ, so that each is in some way already understood to be a divine altar, the reading is a profitable one. For it is fitting that holy men, who have dedicated their own life to Christ, be seen warm and fervent in the Spirit (Romans 12:11), and always so: not sinking into coldness through worldly pleasures, but rather rekindling the mind in holiness toward love of God and desire for virtue. For this is the manner of rational worship (Romans 12:1). This, then, is the meaning of the altar. But he adds a further command that is useful at the literal level as well. He says the ash must be carried out not by someone else, an outsider, that is, someone of another tribe, but rather by the service of those who have been sanctified (Leviticus 6:10–11). Observe how the law allows nothing that belongs to divine service to be thought trivial, or unworthy, as it were, of the priest’s own hands, so that he might hand it over to someone else who is not holy; for the holy things are not open to the unclean. The divine altar itself, too, is not to be touched.
translator_notes: PG 68.821. Palladius answers Cyril’s question at the end of section 20 (was not Emmanuel the altar, in type?). The subject of ἐᾷ (‘does not allow’) is unexpressed; rendered ‘the law’ from context. Leviticus references use English numbering: LXX Lev 6:2–6 = English 6:9–13. ‘Fire came down from heaven upon the altar’ is uncited: Lev 9:24 says the fire came out ‘from the Lord’; the heavenly origin may echo 2 Chronicles 7:1 or tradition, so no citation. ‘The law called the fire the altar’s own’ is a loose paraphrase, cited to Lev 6:9 (‘the fire of the altar’). John 1:32 as Cyril quotes it adds ‘in the form of a dove’ (ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς), language closer to Luke 3:22. Matthew 3:11 has the same words as Luke 3:16. Malachi 3:2–3 follows the LXX (‘herb of washers’, rendered ‘fullers’ soap’). ζέοντας τῷ Πνεύματι echoes Romans 12:11; λατρεία λογική picks up Romans 12:1, quoted at the end of section 20. The ash rule paraphrases Lev 6:10–11, where the priest himself removes the ash; ἀλλογενής (‘one of another race’) may echo Num 3:10 / 18:7, left uncited. The first words of col. 824 (ἐστι θυσιαστήριον, ‘is … altar’) are rendered at the end of this section so the sentence is whole; section 22 starts with the next sentence.

title: Sacred vestments kept from common use; the law of the grain offering
english: Cyril: And so that those chosen for sacred service may know the surpassing holiness of the divine altar, he attaches reverence even to the sacred vestments themselves. For with wise provision he does not allow them to appear outside the tent in their sacred dress. For he means: let not the holy things, after contact with the unclean and carrying defilement from what is foreign, wrong the reverence due to the holy tent. For this reason he directs them to gather the ash dressed in sacred vesture, but to change their clothes when they carry it outside and leave the holy places (Leviticus 6:10–11). A command akin to this was also given through the voice of Ezekiel, who writes thus: ‘And he said to me: The chambers on the north and the chambers on the south, which face the open spaces, these are the chambers of the sanctuary, in which the priests, the sons of Zadok, who draw near to the Lord, to the most holy things, shall eat; and there they shall lay the most holy things and the grain offerings, and the offerings for sin and the offerings for ignorance, for the place is holy. No one shall enter except the priests; they shall not go out from the court of the sanctuary into the outer court, so that those who bring the offerings may be holy always, and may not touch their vestments in which they minister, for these are holy; and they shall put on other garments when they touch the people’ (Ezekiel 42:13–14). So the very vestments of the priests are holy, and kept apart from the common people. And the whole burnt offering burns night and day (Leviticus 6:9–13), for the fragrance of Christ never ceases. And the life of the saints too, if it is understood after the manner of a whole burnt offering, has a fragrance without end; for they give off the fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2:15), offering to God, as priests, what the gospel way of life gives them to boast of, as it were, in works.
Palladius: What you say is true.

Cyril: How the matter of the whole burnt offering stands is not unclear from what we have said. And how the rite of the grain offering, too, may be carried out quite correctly he lays down in these words: ‘This is the law of the grain offering, which the sons of Aaron shall bring before the Lord, in front of the altar. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the offering, with its oil and with all its frankincense that is on the offering; and he shall bring it up on the altar as an offering by fire, a fragrant odor, its memorial to the Lord. And what is left of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place; in the court of the tent of witness they shall eat it. It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it to them as their portion from the Lord’s offerings by fire. It is most holy, like the sin offering and like the guilt offering. Every male among the priests shall eat it. It is a perpetual statute throughout your generations, from the Lord’s offerings by fire. Whoever touches them shall be made holy’ (Leviticus 6:14–18). So the whole burnt offerings signify the complete, so to speak, and entire dedication of those who are especially holy, while the grain offering signifies the life that is holy in part and lived under God.
translator_notes: PG 68.824. The opening words ἐστι θυσιαστήριον complete the last sentence of section 21 and are rendered there. Cyril’s ‘he says’ before ‘let not the holy things…’ introduces his own paraphrase of the law’s intent, not a quotation; rendered ‘he means’. ‘Change their clothes when they carry it outside’ is Lev 6:11 (LXX 6:4). Ezekiel 42:13–14 follows Cyril’s LXX text: where standard LXX has the priests ‘eat the most holy things’, Cyril’s text reads ‘who draw near to the Lord, εἰς the Holy of Holies’; rendered ‘to the most holy things’ to keep the εἰς, so ‘shall eat’ has no stated object, as in his wording. ‘May not touch their vestments’ is literal; the sense is that the vestments must not come into common contact. ‘Night and day’ for the whole burnt offering alludes to Lev 6:9–13 (‘all night until morning’, and the fire kept burning continually); cited as the passage. ‘They give off the fragrance of Christ’ echoes 2 Cor 2:15. In Leviticus θυσία here is the grain offering (minchah); rendered ‘grain offering’ throughout this passage. κάρπωμα rendered ‘offering by fire’; πλημμέλεια ‘guilt offering’. Lev 6:14–18 English = LXX 6:7–11. The first words of col. 825 (μέρους ἁγίαν καὶ ὑπὸ Θεῷ ζωήν) are rendered at the end of this section so the sentence is whole.

title: The grain offering as a life holy in part
english: Cyril: An exact figure of this life is the fine flour offered up in the priest’s handful with the oil and the frankincense. For the life consecrated to God, even if perhaps only in part, must surely be fragrant, and enriched with the richest hopes. Or would you not say that every good work of ours is most fragrant?
Palladius: Certainly.
Cyril: What then? Is it not done by us in good hope?
Palladius: Yes, for what comes from God will surely follow.
Cyril: So the frankincense, and the fine flour moistened with oil, point us to a life that is fragrant and very rich.
Palladius: Well said. But what kind of life among us would be holy in part?

Cyril: One that has not reached the goal of a saintly way of life, and does not walk the path set very high, as perhaps John did, he who was the voice, or the holy apostles; and yet one that does not lose its claim to reverence merely because it perhaps falls short of the lofty path set before us. Or is not the life of those in the world who have children, if they choose to live uprightly, in some way divided between God and the world, in the words of blessed Paul (1 Corinthians 7:33–34)?
Palladius: It is divided; how could it not be?

Cyril: So the partial consecration of the fine flour, which has fragrance and cheerfulness, was a type of the life that is not wholly given over to God, but stands in the middle, as it were, and looks both ways. The law says that this will also be for a memorial (Leviticus 6:15) of the one who brought it through the ministry of the priest. And truly we shall gain this: to be held in God’s remembrance through the things by which we bear fruit and give off fragrance. For Christ acts as mediator and brings to God both the one who is wholly holy, as one ranked among the whole burnt offerings, and the one who is not entirely so, because he is divided and given in part to the world, as a kind of partial offering. The grain offering is unleavened. For it is fitting that whatever we do be done with purity, for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Indeed, the Savior commanded us to shun standing in the middle of the marketplaces to make our prayers (Matthew 6:5), a gloomy face when fasting (Matthew 6:16), and sounding a trumpet unbecomingly when we show mercy to our brothers (Matthew 6:2). For this is leaven, which profanes holy things. What is done for the glory of God should be free of any charge of seeking to please men; for in this way the offering would be truly unleavened and holy. The remainder of the grain offering is a portion and food for the priests. Every male eats it in a holy place (Leviticus 6:16–18). That the holy things are consumed by the priests in a holy place preserves the reverence due to our more mystical teachings; that every male eats it aptly suggests that softness is an ugly thing, and truly unholy, in those whom God has chosen. For softness makes a man unholy, cuts him off from spiritual blessing, and leaves him without share in the good things God has allotted to the saints.
translator_notes: PG 68.825. The opening words (‘part holy and under God life’) complete the last sentence of section 22 and are rendered there; this section begins with the relative clause ἧς ὑποτύπωσις, rendered as a fresh sentence. Doubtful reading: ὁποία τις ἦν ἡ Ἰωάννου φωνὴ τυχόν is literally ‘such as perhaps was the voice of John’; taken as John the Baptist, who called himself ‘the voice’ (John 1:23), uncited because the wording is uncertain. Also uncertain: λῆξις (‘end, completion’) rendered ‘completion’; τῆς ἄγαν ὑποκειμένης, set against ἄγαν ἀνῳκισμένην, is taken as ‘the lofty path set before us’; the sense is that a partly holy life does not lose its claim to reverence by falling short of the highest one. ‘Divided between God and the world’ cites 1 Cor 7:33–34 (μεμέρισται). ‘For the glory of God’ echoes 1 Cor 10:31. Matthew 6:5 speaks of synagogues and street corners; Cyril says ‘marketplaces’, a loose allusion. ‘This is leaven’ may echo Luke 12:1 (leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy); left uncited. Grammatically ‘every male is eaten’ (ἐσθίεται πᾶν ἀρσενικόν) plainly means ‘every male eats it’ (Lev 6:16, 18). μαλακισμός rendered ‘softness’ (weakness of will, unmanliness), which Cyril links to Judas in section 24. The first word of col. 828 (ἀγαθῶν, ‘good things’) is rendered at the end of this section to finish the sentence.

title: Judas’s softness, and the priest’s grain offering wholly burnt
english: Cyril: Judas too grew soft, and turned aside to greed for shameful gain; and this came from an unmanly and ignoble way of thinking. That is why he has remained without any taste of the good things that come from God, and wholly without share in the gifts given to the saints.
Palladius: So it is.

Cyril: This, then, is the law for the offering from the common flock. But he commanded that the offering from the priestly race be brought in another way, saying: ‘This is the gift of Aaron and his sons, which they shall offer to the Lord on the day when you anoint him: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a perpetual grain offering, half of it in the morning and half of it in the evening. It shall be made with oil in a pan; he shall bring it kneaded, in rolls, a grain offering of broken pieces, a grain offering for a fragrant odor to the Lord. The anointed priest who succeeds him from among his sons shall make it. It is a perpetual law; all of it shall be offered. And every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burnt; it shall not be eaten’ (Leviticus 6:20–23). See, Palladius, how exact the law is, and how finely it provides for the safety proper to holy things. Since he commanded that the offerings of the common flock should not be wholly burnt, because these people do not have a life that is entirely holy, but one divided, as it were, between God and the world, he rightly makes a distinction: he places those chosen for sacred service in the higher rank, and says that the offering made for them must be wholly burnt, as they burn to God as incense the fine flour that is brought, morning and evening, that is, through the whole day and at every season. For the chosen man is always, in some sense, holy, and has a fragrance that never ceases, a spiritual one, clearly. He is not divided between God and the world, as some are, but is in constant attendance and without distraction (1 Corinthians 7:35), wholly and entirely devoted to his own Master, and crying out, as it were: ‘I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me’ (Galatians 2:20). The tenth of the fine flour, then, would be a sign of a life that gives off fragrance to God at every season. But ‘in a pan,’ he says, and ‘kneaded with oil,’ and ‘he shall bring it in broken pieces’ (Leviticus 6:21). In a veiled way these signify to us: the pan, I think, what is painful; the kneading with oil, abundance joined with cheerfulness; the broken pieces, the tender and, so to speak, easily broken heart of the saints. For the life that is entirely and wholly holy will surely have to be lived amid toils, will have abundant hope in God, and will have a heart very easily broken; for hardness would least befit it. For it is written: ‘A broken and humbled heart God will not despise’ (Psalm 51:17). But the devil’s heart is set fast like a stone, and like an anvil that cannot be beaten (Job 41:24), for so Holy Scripture says. The law also extends through all time, fulfilled in the succession of those who serve as priests; for one must follow…
translator_notes: PG 68.828. The first word of this column (ἀγαθῶν) is rendered at the end of section 23. Judas’s ‘shameful gain’ may recall John 12:6 but quotes nothing; uncited. ἀγέλη / ἀγελαῖοι (‘the flock’, ‘those of the flock’) here means the general body of the people as opposed to the priestly race (ἱερὸν γένος), not animal offerings; rendered ‘the common flock’. Lev 6:20–23 English = LXX 6:13–16; ἑλικτά rendered ‘in rolls’, θυσία ἐκ κλασμάτων ‘a grain offering of broken pieces’, ὁ ἱερεὺς ὁ χριστός ‘the anointed priest’ (lower-case: Aaron’s successor, not Christ). εὐπαρέδρως καὶ ἀπερισπάστως is the wording of 1 Cor 7:35 (literally ‘assiduously and undistractedly’); ‘serves’ carries the sense of εὐπάρεδρος (‘sitting constantly beside’), with no object added. Galatians 2:20 uses common English numbering (NA28 places ‘I have been crucified with Christ’ at 2:19). Psalm 51:17 = LXX Psalm 50:19. ‘The devil’s heart … like an anvil that cannot be beaten’ is LXX Job 41:15–16 (Rahlfs 41:16), said there of the dragon/Leviathan, which Cyril reads as the devil; English Bible numbering Job 41:24 (Hebrew 41:16). ‘Hardness’ renders τὸ ἀτριβές (‘the unworn, unbroken’). The section ends mid-word (προλαβόν-), so the English stops at ‘one must follow…’ and section 25 supplies ‘the good record of those who went before them’.

title: The priest’s whole offering, and Christ as the sin offering
english: Cyril: …the good record of those who went before them, and show themselves imitators of the fathers' glory, following in the footsteps of their worship and bringing to God the fragrance dearest to him, not in part but wholly. For this, I think, is what is meant by ‘Every sacrifice of a priest shall be wholly burnt’ (Leviticus 6:23).
Palladius: Then we shall offer ourselves and be dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma, following in the footsteps of the saints’ life and keeping to their sacred rites, the spiritual ones, plainly.

Cyril: Certainly, Palladius. But to wipe away defilement and escape from sin could not come about or be found in anyone in any other way than through Christ alone, in whom and through whom is all cleansing, who endured the saving slaughter for us. One may learn this without going far, from the decree that stands next to it and is joined to it. It runs thus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall slaughter the sin offerings before the Lord; they are most holy. The priest who offers it shall eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the tent of witness. Everyone who touches its flesh shall be made holy; and if any of its blood is sprinkled on a garment, whatever it is sprinkled on shall be washed in a holy place. And an earthen vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken; but if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, he shall scour it and rinse it with water. Every male among the priests shall eat them; they are most holy to the Lord’ (Leviticus 6:24–29).

The victim for sin, then, could be none other than Emmanuel, who is the true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). And he is slaughtered in the place of the whole burnt offering. For Christ is not holy in part, as we are, for he committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22); he is wholly fragrant and sacred, and the giver of holiness to all others. For even if he was reckoned among the lawless (Isaiah 53:12) and, in the divine plan, was counted among the condemned, the Father knows the death of the Son to be holy and sacred. That is why he says: ‘In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall slaughter the sin offering also; it is most holy’ (Leviticus 6:25). For just as the Son is God of gods, so also is he Holy of holies, himself making the whole creation holy by his own Spirit, since he is by nature from the Father and is truly God.

The priest who brings the sacrifice, he says, shall eat it. For each one, I think, who has been brought into the sacred ministry will gather the fruit of his own labors and reap the reward of his own service. And what remains of the sacrifice is eaten in holy places and in the court of the holy tent (Leviticus 6:26). For the mysteries are offered in churches, and in them the chosen race is counted worthy of the holy table of Christ. And wherever a lawful priest serves, the place will be holy. And the sacrifice makes holy the one who touches it, and so does the sprinkling of the blood (Leviticus 6:27). For we draw near…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: the clause began at the end of §24 ('one must follow the [good record] of those who went before'); the fragment 'των εὐδοκιμήσεσι' is rendered 'the good record of those who went before them'. Ends mid-word on 'Προσ', completed as 'Προσίεμεν' at the head of §26, so the English breaks at 'For we draw near…'. Leviticus references use English numbering; Rahlfs LXX numbers these verses 6:16 (=Eng. 6:23) and 6:17-22 (=Eng. 6:24-29). In 6:23 LXX θυσία renders the Hebrew grain offering; kept as 'sacrifice' because Cyril reads it of the priest's self-offering. 'οὐ γὰρ ἐποίησεν ἁμαρτίαν' matches 1 Peter 2:22 (cf. Isaiah 53:9); 'ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη' is Isaiah 53:12 (quoted in Luke 22:37). 'Θεὸς θεῶν' is a scriptural title (Deuteronomy 10:17; Psalm 50:1 [LXX 49:1]; Psalm 136:2 [LXX 135:2]) but no single source is clear, so it is uncited. 'τὸ ἀπόλεκτον γένος' may echo 1 Peter 2:9 (γένος ἐκλεκτόν) but the wording differs; uncited. 'τῷ ἰδίῳ πνεύματι' taken as the Holy Spirit, proper to the Son (Cyril's usage), hence 'his own Spirit'. The earlier listing of 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Hebrews 13:10 for this section is not supported by the Greek and is dropped.

title: The guilt offering and the parts reserved for God
english: Cyril: …to the holy things for no other reason than to share in the holy Christ through the ineffable and spiritual sacrifice. And the vessels that serve the sacrifices are also purified (Leviticus 6:28), so that what has served sacred things may belong to nothing else and not be put to human uses. This law has been kept, and it is preserved in the churches. And the law will again make clear that being blessed befits those who act with manly courage, when it says: ‘Every male among the priests shall eat them’ (Leviticus 6:29).
Palladius: The point is clear.

Cyril: Besides this, he also lays down how the sacrifice should be properly carried out (the sacrifice for sin, I mean): which parts of it the ministers may eat, and which are set apart for a fragrant aroma. For it is written thus: ‘And all the sin offerings, any of whose blood is brought into the tent of witness to make atonement in the holy place, shall not be eaten; it shall be burned up in fire (Leviticus 6:30). And this is the law of the ram of the guilt offering; it is most holy. In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall slaughter the ram of the guilt offering before the Lord. And he shall pour its blood at the base of the altar all around. And he shall offer from it all its fat: the loin, and all the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat on the entrails, and the two kidneys and the fat on them that is on the thighs, and the lobe on the liver with the kidneys; he shall remove them, and the priest shall offer them on the altar as an offering to the Lord; it is a guilt offering. Every male of the priests shall eat them; they shall eat them in a holy place; they are most holy. As the sin offering is, so is the guilt offering; there is one law for them. The priest who makes atonement with it shall have it’ (Leviticus 7:1–7).

For he declares that the inward parts of the victims must not be made into food. They must, he says, be dedicated to God alone and offered to him. This, I think, is what ‘it shall be burned up in fire’ points to; that is, what is dedicated is to be plainly assigned to the divine nature alone, which is above all things, and of which fire is a type. And when the ram of the guilt offering is sacrificed, its blood is poured out at the base of the altar; for the death of Christ is holy and sacred, and fragrant as well. For the inward parts are offered up: the fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver. These, I think, as I have said elsewhere too, would be a type of virtue, not of one virtue only but of many kinds. For the ways of virtue are very many. And so we have been justified in Christ, who endured death for us and dedicated himself to God the Father as a fragrant aroma (Ephesians 5:2).

He makes clear that we shall not serve God without reward, for he says straight after this: ‘And the priest who offers someone’s whole burnt offering, the skin of the whole burnt offering that he offers shall be his; and every sacrifice that is prepared in the oven, and every one that is prepared…’ (Leviticus 7:8–9)
translator_notes: Opens mid-word: 'Προσ' at the end of §25 + 'ίεμεν' here = 'we draw near'. Ends mid-quotation; Leviticus 7:9 continues in §27 ('…on a grill or in a pan'). Leviticus 6:30 in English numbering is LXX 6:23 (Rahlfs). 'κριὸς τῆς πλημμελείας' follows the LXX, which supplies 'ram' at Leviticus 7:1 where the Hebrew has only 'guilt offering'. 'ὀσφύς' rendered 'loin' following the LXX (Hebrew: the fat tail). 'κάρπωμα' rendered 'an offering'. The clause 'τοῦτ' ἔστιν, ἀνακεῖσθαι τὸ ἐν μόνῃ ἐκνενεμήσθω σαφῶς τῇ θείᾳ… φύσει' is grammatically rough in the Migne text (likely corrupt); rendered by its evident sense: what is dedicated is assigned to the divine nature alone, of which fire is a type. 'ἐνδόσθια' in Cyril's comment: he seems to extend the burned sin offering (6:30) to the inward parts set apart for God in 7:3-5; translated literally as 'inward parts'. 'Ἀνδριζομένοις' (acting manfully) may echo 1 Corinthians 16:13 (ἀνδρίζεσθε) but this is doubtful; uncited. 'δεδικαιώμεθα ἐν Χριστῷ' is Pauline language (cf. Galatians 2:17; Romans 5:9) without a single clear source; uncited. The fragrant self-offering to God the Father matches Ephesians 5:2 (προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν τῷ θεῷ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας), cited.

title: Equal shares for the priests and the sacrifice of praise
english: Cyril: …on a grill or in a pan shall belong to the priest who offers it. And every sacrifice mixed with oil, and every one not mixed, shall belong to all the sons of Aaron, to each an equal share’ (Leviticus 7:9–10). This law too is preserved in the churches, and it secures equality for those who serve at the altar, giving each, without variation, his portion of the bloodless sacrifice. Knowing this, Paul writes: ‘So also the Lord commanded that those who attend the altar should live from the altar’ (1 Corinthians 9:13–14). And those who offer the sacrifices are sharers in the altar, as he himself says again somewhere (1 Corinthians 10:18).
Palladius: That is so.

Cyril: He also regulates the sacrifice of praise and directs how it is to be done, saying: ‘This is the law of the sacrifice of salvation that they shall offer to the Lord. If he offers it for praise, then with the sacrifice of praise he shall offer loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil, and fine flour kneaded with oil. With loaves of leavened bread he shall offer his gifts, along with the sacrifice of salvation offered in praise. And he shall bring one out of all his gifts as a portion set apart for the Lord; it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the sacrifice of salvation. And the meat of the sacrifice of salvation offered in praise shall be his, and it shall be eaten on the day it is offered; they shall not leave any of it until morning’ (Leviticus 7:11–15). He has commanded that the sacrifice of praise be made with leavened loaves, even though elsewhere he said clearly and plainly: ‘You shall offer no leaven and no honey to the Lord your God. You shall offer them to the Lord as a gift of firstfruits, but they shall not be put on the altar for a fragrant aroma to the Lord’ (Leviticus 2:11–12). Would you not say, then, Palladius, that looking closely into these things brings profit?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: What, then, is the meaning of this arrangement? Come, let us say, searching it out as far as we can and opening up the hidden path. So, very much in keeping with the law, the inspired David too, striking up the spiritual lyre, says: ‘I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord’ (Psalm 116:13), and so expressly calls the sacrifice of praise a cup of salvation. And we too offer praise in great numbers in the churches, in unity of spirit, brought together through faith as into one body (Ephesians 4:3–4) and one soul. For it is written: ‘The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul’ (Acts 4:32). We also often give glory alone, quietly at home, by day and by night; and this is the habit of good people. Or is what I say not true?
Palladius: How could it not be?

Cyril: But whether the offering is brought by us in the churches in great numbers, or is performed in other places, perhaps by one alone, or by two somewhere, or three, or more still, no distinction is drawn among those present who are accustomed to sing hymns and have gathered for this. For together with those already cleansed through holy baptism there joins in offering the sacrifice…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation (Leviticus 7:8-10, begun at the end of §26). Ends mid-sentence: the subject of 'συναναφέρει' is 'ὁ κατηχούμενος' (the catechumen) at the head of §28, so the English breaks at 'there joins in offering the sacrifice…'. LXX Leviticus 7:10 reads 'mixed with oil and not mixed' where the Hebrew has 'mixed with oil or dry'; the LXX wording is kept. In Leviticus 7:12 the Migne text prints 'ἄρτους ἓξ σεμιδάλεως' ('six loaves'); the LXX reads 'ἄρτους ἐκ σεμιδάλεως' ('loaves of fine flour') and 'ἓξ' is almost certainly a misprint, so 'loaves of fine flour' is translated. 'θυσία σωτηρίου' is the LXX term for the peace offering; rendered 'sacrifice of salvation' because Cyril's argument links it to the 'cup of salvation' (ποτήριον σωτηρίου). Paul's words are a conflation of 1 Corinthians 9:13 and 9:14 (the Lord commanded those who proclaim the gospel to live by the gospel), so both verses are cited. 'κοινωνοὶ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου' matches 1 Corinthians 10:18. Cyril's Leviticus 2:11-12 quotation is loose against the LXX. Psalm 116:13 in English numbering = LXX Psalm 115:4. 'εἰς ἑνότητα πνεύματος… ἓν σῶμα' echoes Ephesians 4:3-4 (unity of the Spirit, one body); cited as a clear allusion, but Cyril writes 'one body and one soul', blending it with Acts 4:32; lower-case 'spirit' kept because the phrase here stresses the believers' concord. 'κατὰ δύο… καὶ τρεῖς' may echo Matthew 18:20 (two or three gathered) but the wording is not close; uncited. 'Ἆρ' οὖν… οὐκ ὀνησιφόρον εἶναι φής' is a question expecting assent, rendered positively ('Would you not say… is meant for our profit?') so that Palladius's 'Very much so' keeps its sense. 'τὸ περίεργον ἐν τούτοις' taken as close inquiry into these things (the activity Cyril at once resumes with 'πολυπραγμονοῦντες'), not as 'the curious point'; either reading leaves Palladius's assent intact.

title: Leavened and unleavened bread in the sacrifice of praise
english: Cyril: …the catechumen too, who is still under instruction; and after he has offered the praise together with the perfect, he withdraws from the more sacred mysteries and is kept from the sacrifice that is in Christ. This is why the law did well to foretell this arrangement, when it commanded that the sacrifice of praise be made with leavened loaves and with unleavened wafers (Leviticus 7:12–13). Each of the things named, I think, points to a kind of life. The leavened bread will be a type of a life not yet cleansed through holy baptism, nor yet wholly freed from the world’s uncleanness. The unleavened wafer is a type of the life already washed clean in Christ through faith: the life of the perfect, I mean, whom the inspired Paul also addressed when he said: ‘Let us therefore keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth’ (1 Corinthians 5:8). And again: ‘So cleanse out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened’ (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Palladius: Very well said.

Cyril: Besides these, the fine flour, not yet brought together into one mass as it is in a loaf or a wafer, but still remaining, as it were, in its grains, hints that each of those who offer the praise does so as one by himself. For we are acceptable to God when we give him glory both each of us on our own and all of us together as one company. Oil is poured on the sacrifice of praise, signifying the gladness of the act, and that mercy from God will in every way and without fail follow those who are accustomed to offer it. For it says: ‘Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your affliction, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me’ (Psalm 50:14–15). And the disciple of Christ also writes: ‘Is anyone among you downcast? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise’ (James 5:13). So the law clearly showed in figure that the sacrifice of praise must be carried out with leavened loaves, with unleavened wafers, and with fine flour still in its grains. One portion of each was brought forward (Leviticus 7:14), and of the fine flour, as it were, a single handful; a sheep was slaughtered and its inner parts were burnt according to the law; and the rest was food for those appointed to serve as priests, the law thus showing that the priesthood does not go unrewarded. And it adds a further command: ‘On the day it is offered it shall be eaten; they shall not leave any of it until the morning’ (Leviticus 7:15). Through this, again, we may perhaps understand something like this: when the time has run its course, and the present age has passed like a day, another manner of giving glory, beyond those we know, will be devised for us. For just as those under the law, when they had been set free from Pharaoh’s tyranny, said with joy: ‘Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been greatly glorified; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea’ (Exodus 15:1); and just as some of the saints, foreseeing in the Spirit the achievements of our Savior’s coming, which are incomparably brighter and greater, cried aloud: ‘Sing to the Lord a new song’ (Psalm 98:1), and this was: ‘God has gone up with a shout’ (Psalm 47:5), when he had despoiled Hades, ‘and said
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence: ὁ κατηχούμενος is the subject of συναναφέρει at the end of section 27 ('there joins in offering the sacrifice…'), so the English opens with the catechumen and does not repeat the verb. Leviticus 7:12–13 LXX supplies the terms: θυσία αἰνέσεως (the thank offering, here 'sacrifice of praise'), λάγανα ἄζυμα (7:12), σεμίδαλις (7:12), ἄρτοι ζυμῖται (7:13); κεγχρεμίς is 'grain' (of flour). Cyril quotes 1 Corinthians 5:8 before 5:7; kept in his order. The oil (ἔλαιον) and mercy (ἐλεεῖσθαι) pairing is a sound play in Greek that English cannot keep. Psalm 50:14–15 = LXX Psalm 49:14–15. James 5:13: Cyril reads Ἀθυμεῖ ('downcast') where the New Testament text has Κακοπαθεῖ ('suffering'); translated as he reads. 'One portion of each' = Leviticus 7:14 (ἓν ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν δώρων). 'A single handful' (ὡς ἐν δρακὶ μιᾷ) recalls the grain-offering handful of Leviticus 2:2, but the link to the thank offering is loose, so it is left uncited; the slaughtered sheep and burnt entrails summarise the peace-offering rite of Leviticus 3, also left uncited. ἐν νόμῳ with ἔλεγον rendered 'those under the law' (the people in the time of the law). 'Sing to the Lord a new song' is word for word in LXX Psalms 95:1, 97:1 and 149:1 (English 96:1, 98:1, 149:1); cited as Psalm 98:1 (LXX 97:1) because its next words ('for He has done marvelous things … His right hand has saved') match Cyril's 'achievements', but Psalm 96:1 is equally possible. Psalm 47:5 = LXX Psalm 46:6. 'When He had despoiled Hades' (σκυλεύσας τὸν ᾅδην) is Cyril's own gloss between two quotations, so it stands outside the quotation marks. ἐν πνεύματι rendered 'in the Spirit' (prophetic sight). The sentence runs on into section 29 with Isaiah 49:9; the closing 'in the same way' comes there. Exodus 15:1 LXX ἐνδόξως δεδόξασται rendered 'He has been greatly glorified' (not the calque 'gloriously glorified'). εἰπών closing the sentence is rendered 'and said' so it runs on from 'when He had despoiled Hades'.

title: Fuller praise to come, and the priests’ share of the offerings
english: Cyril: …to those in bonds, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves”’ (Isaiah 49:9): in the same way, I think, once death has been abolished and sin wholly undone, there will be a manner of praise fitting that time. For we shall sing hymns for greater things; and, made rich with good things beyond mind and speech, we shall crown Christ, the giver of all good things to us, with brighter praises, together with God the Father. For it says: ‘Whether there are prophecies, they will be abolished; whether there is knowledge, it will cease. Now we know in part; but when what is perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished’ (1 Corinthians 13:8–10). And Christ himself also said: ‘These things I have spoken to you in figures; but the hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in figures, but shall tell you plainly about the Father’ (John 16:25). Since, then, a more perfect knowledge will be in us when its time comes, we shall also sing hymns more loftily than now.
Palladius: The argument is convincing.

Cyril: Having laid down for each sacrifice the rule that fits it, and having explained very well how it should be done, he at once makes the priest a sharer in the altar. For it is written thus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: You and your sons and your father’s house shall take the firstfruits of the holy things; and you and your sons shall take the sins of your priesthood’ (Numbers 18:1). Then he adds that they must hold to their sacred tasks with a wakeful and sober mind (Numbers 18:2–7), and says: ‘And behold, I Myself have given you the keeping of the firstfruits from all that is consecrated to me by the sons of Israel; to you I have given them as a privilege, and to your sons after you, a perpetual ordinance. And this shall be yours from the consecrated holy things of the burnt offerings: from all their gifts, and from all their sacrifices, and from every trespass of theirs, and from all their sins, all that they render to me from all the holy things shall belong to you and to your sons. In the Holy of Holies you shall eat them; every male shall eat them, you and your sons. They shall be holy to you. And this shall be yours from the firstfruits of their gifts, from all the wave offerings of the sons of Israel. To you I have given them, and to your sons and your daughters with you, a perpetual ordinance; everyone who is clean in your house shall eat them. All the firstfruits of oil, and all the firstfruits of wine and of grain, the firstfruits of whatever they give to the Lord, I have given to you. All the first produce that is in their land, whatever they bring to the Lord, shall be yours; everyone who is clean in your house shall eat them. Everything devoted among the sons of Israel shall be yours; and everything that opens the womb, of all flesh, whatever they offer to the Lord, from man to beast, shall be yours. But the firstborn of men shall surely be redeemed with a ransom, and the firstborn of unclean beasts you shall redeem. Its redemption shall be from a month old; the valuation is five shekels, by the holy shekel; it is twenty obols (Numbers 18:8–16). But the firstborn
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation: Isaiah 49:9 LXX (λέγοντα τοῖς ἐν δεσμοῖς Ἐξέλθατε, καὶ τοῖς ἐν τῷ σκότει ἀνακαλυφθῆναι), joined by Cyril to Psalm 47:5 in section 28; 'in the same way' closes the 'just as' comparison begun there. 'Together with God the Father' (συστεφανώσομεν τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρί): Christ is crowned with praise along with the Father. 1 Corinthians 13:8–10: Cyril's text says knowledge 'will cease' (παύσεται, the verb Paul uses of tongues) and 'now (ἄρτι) we know in part', which blends 13:9 with 13:12; translated as he reads. John 16:25: παροιμίαι rendered 'figures'; Cyril reads οὔτε for οὐκέτι, rendered 'no longer'. Numbers 18:1: Cyril's text reads 'the firstfruits (ἀπαρχάς) of the holy things' where the LXX has 'the sins (ἁμαρτίας) of the holy things'; translated as he reads. λήψεσθε is kept as 'take' (the Hebrew sense is 'bear the iniquity'), because in section 30 Cyril reads 'sins' as the sin offerings the priests receive. Numbers 18:2–7 (the Levites' and priests' charge over the sanctuary) is summarised, not quoted. The long quotation runs from Numbers 18:8 to 18:19 and is split by the source at 18:17 ('But the firstborn'); it closes in section 30. καρπώματα rendered 'burnt offerings'; ἐπιθέματα rendered 'wave offerings' (the LXX term for the Hebrew tenuphah); 'twenty obols' follows the LXX (Hebrew: twenty gerahs). The subject of 'makes the priest a sharer in the altar' is God as lawgiver, understood from the context. Isaiah 49:9 ἀνακαλύφθητε rendered 'Show yourselves' (literally 'be uncovered', that is, come out into the light). The emphatic ἐγώ of Numbers 18:8 is kept as 'I Myself'.

title: Sin offerings called ‘sin’, and food for the priest’s household
english: Cyril: …of calves, the firstborn of sheep, and the firstborn of goats you shall not redeem; they are holy. You shall pour their blood against the altar, and offer up the fat as a burnt offering, for a fragrant aroma to the Lord. And their meat shall be yours, like the breast of the wave offering; and like the right shoulder it shall be yours. Every portion set apart from the holy things, whatever the sons of Israel set apart for the Lord, I have given to you and to your sons and your daughters with you, a perpetual ordinance; it is a covenant of everlasting salt before the Lord, for you and your offspring after you’ (Numbers 18:17–19). From this too, then, you see quite clearly, I think, that he has plainly assigned every kind of sacrifice and offering to the sacred and chosen race, including what comes ‘from every trespass and from all the sins’, that is, the victims offered for every trespass and sin. For the victims offered for sin bear the name ‘sin’. That is why our wise Paul also applied the law’s word to Christ, saying: ‘We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God; for him who knew no sin he made sin for us’ (2 Corinthians 5:20–21). For the Son was sacrificed for our sins according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3), as an innocent lamb (Jeremiah 11:19). That the law gave the name ‘sin’ to the victims offered for our sin, God will make clear when he says through the prophet concerning the priests: ‘They shall eat the sins of my people’ (Hosea 4:8); that is, what is offered for the sins of my people shall be food for the priests. So he assigns to them what remains of every sacrifice, and commands that it be eaten, but only in a holy place, he says, and by every male (Numbers 18:10; Leviticus 7:6). The reason for this we have given in what has gone before. But the firstfruits of oil, grain and wine, the payments for redeeming the firstborn, and the devoted things as well, are to be eaten no longer by the males alone, nor in the holy court, but now in the priest’s house; they are set there for the enjoyment even of his daughters, and of everyone close to him and of his own household. This distinction must be carefully observed. For the remains of the sacrifices would be fitting for the use of the consecrated alone, and will not be common food; and a holy place is the place that befits them. But whatever else is left over, having been brought as a gift, holds, one might say, a second rank of its own once the priest has received it; and it will belong to the priests’ whole household, if only the person is clean, that is, not profane: according to the law, if he is not uncircumcised, not a foreigner, not a leper, not one with a discharge (Leviticus 22:4, 10); but according to the aim of the new Scripture and the Church’s safeguard, if he is not unholy and unbelieving, if he is devout and loves God. For it would be most fitting for those brought into the divine priestly service to love to keep close company with people who are good in character and whose minds are full of love for God. And by adding to this, ‘It is a covenant of everlasting salt before the Lord, for you and your offspring with you’ (Numbers 18:19), he has commanded that what he also said elsewhere be kept without fail (Leviticus 2:13): ‘The salt of the covenant of the Lord shall not be lacking from your sacrifices. With every gift of yours you shall
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation (Numbers 18:17–19, continued from section 29); the closing quotation mark and citation stand at the end of 18:19. In the quotation the covenant is 'for you and your offspring after you' (μετὰ σέ); when Cyril repeats it later the source reads 'with you' (μετὰ σοῦ); both kept as written. ἀφαίρεμα / ἀφέλωσιν rendered 'portion set apart / set apart' (the heave offering). 'Victims offered for sin bear the name sin': in the LXX the sin offering is often called simply ἁμαρτία, which is the ground of Cyril's reading of 2 Corinthians 5:21. 'Sacrificed for our sins according to the Scriptures' echoes 1 Corinthians 15:3 (Cyril has τέθυται, 'was sacrificed', for Paul's ἀπέθανεν, 'died'). 'Innocent lamb' (ἀρνίον ἄκακον) is the exact phrase of LXX Jeremiah 11:19 (ὡς ἀρνίον ἄκακον ἀγόμενον τοῦ θύεσθαι), so it is cited. Hosea 4:8 is a rebuke in its setting; Cyril uses only its wording. 'Only in a holy place … by every male' paraphrases Numbers 18:10, which says 'in the Holy of Holies'. Punctuation: Migne puts a full stop before Ἐν δὴ τοῖς ἤδη παρῳχηκόσιν, but the δέ after ἐλαίου shows the new clause begins there, so the phrase is read with the preceding sentence ('The reason for this we have given in what has gone before'). ἐπιτήρησι in the source is read as ἐπιτήρησιν. Doubtful: παραλαβὼν (masculine nominative singular) has no clear subject in 'Τὰ δὲ ὅσα περίεστιν … παραλαβὼν, δεύτερόν πως, φησὶν, ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἔχει λόγον'; it is rendered 'once the priest has received it', and φησίν is rendered 'one might say', since no Scripture is being quoted; the text may be corrupt here. Leviticus 22:4 (leper, man with a discharge) and 22:10 (no foreigner may eat the holy things) are cited; 'uncircumcised' comes from Exodus 12:43–48 (the Passover) and is left uncited, since Leviticus 22 does not name it. τοῦ νέου Γράμματος rendered 'the new Scripture'. Leviticus 2:13 quotation runs on into section 31 ('…offer salt to the Lord your God'); its citation is placed before the quotation because the quotation ends in the next section. τοῖς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίας θύμασιν rendered 'the victims offered for our sin' (ἡμῶν kept). 'Only in a holy place … by every male' matches Leviticus 7:6 (the trespass offering: 'every male among the priests shall eat it; in a holy place it shall be eaten') word for word, so it is cited beside Numbers 18:10.

title: Salt on the offering, sober priests, and the law that teaches Christ
english: Cyril: ‘…you shall offer salt to the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 2:13). The sacrifice was sprinkled with salt, the type signifying that one must be consecrated to God with understanding, and make one’s approach to him, as it were, most savoury. For bread will not be eaten without salt, as it is written (Job 6:6). Christ said to the holy apostles: ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13).
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: These, then, are the laws by which those who have been sanctified ought to serve as priests. But those who have been chosen, on whom the best verdict has fallen, must keep away both from profane company and from worldly care. Through such care even a steady mind may become drunk, and all but be toppled into improper pleasures. He makes this clear when he says in Leviticus: ‘You shall not drink wine or strong drink, you and your sons with you, whenever you go into the tent of witness or approach the altar, so that you do not die. It is a perpetual statute throughout your generations, to distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the unclean and the clean. And you shall teach the sons of Israel all the statutes that the Lord spoke to them by the hand of Moses’ (Leviticus 10:9–11).

See, then, that they must keep awake. To handle the sacred liturgy with a darkened mind, and with an anxious heart that is drunk with worldly things, brings death; for some are drunk without wine. For at times the mind, unable to walk upright, slips away toward what is unseemly; the sacred things fall into disarray, and what is performed is no longer in good order but is thrown, as it were, off the straight road. Those who suffer this cannot help but offend God and endure bitter penalties for their carelessness. So one must keep awake and shake off the drunkenness that comes from worldly care. The Savior himself also urges this when he says: ‘Take care that your hearts are not weighed down by anxiety and the cares of this life’ (Luke 21:34).

What our way of sobriety would be, and how we shall remain unprofaned and clean and free of punishment, he indicated at once. For ‘distinguish,’ He says, ‘between holy and profane, and between clean and unclean; and you shall teach the sons of Israel all the statutes that the Lord spoke by the hand of Moses’ (Leviticus 10:10–11). This plainly means that the priests, having shaken off drunkenness, ought to keep away from men who are not holy but profane and unclean. And I think a man would do this very easily if he is himself unprofaned and clean; for ‘every living creature,’ it says, ‘loves its like, and a man will cling to one like himself’ (Sirach 13:15–16).

Besides this, they ought to be wise and able to teach; for whoever has charge of the rational flock must be sober and able to teach (1 Timothy 3:2). He puts it very well when he says, ‘You shall teach,’ that is, ‘You shall make plain,’ so that the hearers may be able to see that the law is a tutor (Galatians 3:24) and speaks the mystery of Christ. For nothing in it is hard to grasp or needs teaching, unless it is understood spiritually; for the historical account is entirely simple and free of the shadows of obscurity.
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation: the end of Leviticus 2:13 LXX ('upon every gift of yours you shall offer salt to the Lord your God'), begun at the close of section 30. 'Bread will not be eaten without salt' is Job 6:6 LXX, which asks it as a question; Cyril cites it as a statement. Leviticus 10:9–11 follows the LXX closely (σικερα = strong drink; συμβιβάσεις = 'you shall teach'). Cyril's form of Luke 21:34 has 'anxiety and cares of this life' (φροντίδι καὶ μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς) in place of the standard 'dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life'. Sirach 13:15–16 joins two LXX verses. 'Sober and apt to teach' for one over the flock is a clear allusion to 1 Timothy 3:2 (νηφάλιον ... διδακτικόν). 'The law is a tutor' alludes to Galatians 3:24 (παιδαγωγός). 'Some are drunk without wine' may echo Isaiah 29:9 or 51:21 LXX, but the wording is not close enough; left uncited. OCR: μέθνη read as μέθην. In the last sentence I punctuate δυσέφικτον γὰρ οὐδὲν ἢ συμβιβασμοῦ δεόμενον as one clause (the printed full stop before ἢ looks like an error). 'Ἐν κόσμῳ' is rendered 'in good order'. The sentence beginning Ἄθρει is compressed in the Greek; I take θανάτου πρόξενον as predicate of τὸ λειτουργίας ἅπτεσθαι τῆς ἱερᾶς, with 'some are drunk without wine' as a parenthesis.
